div.p: ALWAYS USE McDOUGALL'S Patent SELF-RAISING FLOUR IT IS THE BEST. The Examiner, WOMAN'S REALM. THE BLACK DRESS-FASHION-HOME. ; MOTOR CAR. By J.B. BARRIS BURLAND.

The Leveson Gosvers.—The Duke and Duchess of Sutherland will not be in any difficulties about another home, if the Duke should carry out his threat to shut up the stately Trentham Hall, in consequence of the foul condition of the river Trent, which flows through the grounds. The Duke has long threatened to take this course, but it has not been regarded very seriously, any more than was the Duke of Devonshire's threat to shut up Chatsworthin consequence of the Death Duties Budget in 1894. The Duke of Sutherland owns, in area of land, nearly a fortieth part of the whole of the whole of Britain, and possesses the finest house in London as well as one of the finest seats in Scotland at Dunrobin Castle. The Gower family is ancient and historic, but up to a century and a half ago, the Gowers were simply Yorkshire squires. As in the case of the Grosvenors, the Howsrds, and the Hamiltons, wealth and titles came to them by marriage. There has been at least three Gower marriages which have brought great riches into the family, which besides the dukedom possess five baronies, four viscounties five earldoms and a marquisaie. The Modern Housewife.—lt has been said that no one can indiet a nation, but if Dr. Allbutt, Regius Professor of Physic at Cambridge is to be accepted as an autho- rity, housekeeping is becoming a lost art in this country. He makes a distinction in favour of the Scottish housewife, who, he thinks, is more homely, more thrifty, and generally more successful, but,for the rest, he says there has been a grievous decline in the standard of housekeeping. Dr. Allbutt is no doubt justified in this view, as it is obvious that as women have taken a larger share in the business and pleasures of life, so they have become less of a machine for housecleaning, and cooking at home. It is in the towns and cities that the difference between old and modern conditions of life is so marked, but it is certain that the change is a permanent one, and that, if we are to look for a solution, it must be in the direction of labour saving appliances and inventions, which will simplify the task and routine of household economy. Beware of Shop-keeper's Labels.—Purchasers at the sales should be a little more careful than usual in removing the price tickets, and announcements of wonderful reductions, and so on, which shop-keepers so liberally affix to their wares in the sale season. A certain lady, who was a gueat at a fashionable wedding in London the other day, is now painfully aware of the need for a little care:in this direction. She was wear- ing a very charming hat, but her self-conscious pride was quickly changed to embarrassment,lwhen she became aware that it still bore aloft the legend "Reduced from" Ste. Most women in ordinary circumstances would be safe from such a disaster, because "a bargain bat" would be so much quizzed, tried on, and ehewn to one's friends, that it would be impossible for the ticket to be overlooked, but this poor lady ,had evidently relied upon her maid, and it is certain that the maid afterwards had a very bad quarter of an hour. Fashionable Ornaments.—Earrings have evidently come to stay, and the majority of fashionable women, now don these ornaments as regularly as they do their rings. Among the ladies of our Royal Family earrings have always been in favour. From quite a young girl, the Princess of 'Vaies has worn earrings of the stud variety, while Princess Henry of Battenberg has always preferred, and invariably worn, the pendant style. Princess Victoria, Princess Ems of Battenberg, Princess Charles of Denmark, and Princess Louise Augusta of Schleswig-Holstein, all wear earrings, either pendant or stud, while Princess Louise, Duchess of Argyle possesses a unique collection of these particular ornaments. Much has been said, for and against the mode—especially against, but the fact remains that the earring is univers- ally becoming, and having realised this truth we are not likely to let the earring go. An Undesirable Exhibition.—With the plain band of lace taking the place of frills and ruches and finishing off our elbow sleeves, the exhibition Of the weakest point in our figures, viz. the elbow, has arrived at a truly distressing stage. Our Parisienne sister sees to it that for outdoor wear her gloves well meet her sleeves, and, unless she possesses really pretty arms, a trans- parent vnder-sleeve, to the wrist, is worn indoors, to veil imperfections. There is no denying the fact that the elbow sleeve with us is not an unqualified success, and lovers of the artistic will rejoice to hear that its reign is likely to end with the summer. New Colors.—Early autumn colours includes number of new plum, purple and red shades, also some exquisite golden wheat tones. Brown contrary to the usual routine, is conspicuous by its absence, and this is pro- bably due to the spring craze for this particular color, which extended almost into the summer. We are some- what tired of brown, and the probability is that it will 'be little in evidence during the coming season. At the moment pale blue reigns supreme, some lovely shades in peacock ranking first in favor. Embroidered Hosiery.—The craze for embroidered stockings continues unabated, but as many of us have discovered they are not the best of wear. Mans- women who have the spare time, nowadays embroider their own stockings, and this is really an easy, end interesting task. The simplest pattern, such as tiny squares with starred centres, spots, and fleur-de-lys, are the best. An excellent plan too, is to draw the stocking on to a wooden boot tree, and then with a warm iron transfer the pattern to the hose. No knots should be made, each end of a length of silk being run through the embroidery both-at start and finish. The embroidery should be worked while the stocking remains upon the tree, and all drawing and puckering will be avoided. The Fan Bouquet.—At two or three Society weddings that have taken place this summer the shower arrange- ment of flowers has given place to the fan bouquet, which, being very light in weight has answered to the double purpose. The fan is formed of wire, to which the flowers are affixed in the most graceful and natural manner possible, long loops and ends of ribbon flowing from the handle. A well-known lady florist is making a speciality of these flower fans. an i she prefers to arrange the blossoms on one side only, covering the wire on the other side,—and the handle—with loops and twistings of silver gauze ribbon. This makes for con- venience when the wearer wishes to lay her fan bouquet down. _ _ _

A More Refined Procedure.—The fashion for wearing a quantity of jewellery in the morning is, happily, among those past and gone. It is no longer deemed correct to cover one's flugers with rings, load one's self with brooches and pendants. hang one's self with chains, and fix quantities of jewelled combs in the hair, when about to take a constitutional, or sally forth on a shopping tour. Less jewellery too is worn in the after- noon, the best dressed women waiting until the evening to display their eems. Queen Alexandra has been wear- ing her magnificent emeralds s great deal during the London season, and this has caused these particular gems to enjoy high favour lately. Lady Ludlow and Lady Londeshorough both possess fine emeralds, while perhaps the best rubies belong to the Duchess of Port- load, Lady Wirnhorne, Lady Stradbrolie, and Mrs. Brad- ley Martin. Lady Dudley cad Mrs. Mackay possess the most wonderful sapphires, the latter's crown and neck- lace of these stones being beautiful beyond compare. MA DOE.
AN EITGL/SII NURSE OF JAPAN'S SOLDIEPS.

A Welsh correspondent says: "Mrs. Teresa Richardson, widow of the late Mr. John Crow Richardson, of Clanbrydan Park, Carmarthen- shire, who is new on her way to Wales after over twelve months' work with the Japanese tick and woundod, has the distinction of being the only English lady who has been with the Japanese Red Cross i!;,,74ety.. She returns loaded with honours. ' In addition to the sixth class Order of the Crown, the highest decoration for ladies in Japan, conferred upon her by the Mikado, and the accepting and wearing of which King Edward has sanctioned. she has received the Order of Merit, the highest order of the Japanese Pert Cross Society, and two other decorations in the shape of medals."

In our sketch is depicted a charming but in- expensive little gown of pale-blue mercerised Lawn, spotted with a ring spot of black. The crossover bodice is edged with white broderie Anglaise, and op.-sns over a vest of white Valenciennes insertion. To give plenty of ful- ness to the frnnt of the bodi'.e, the material is

set in fine gathers at the shoulders. Behind, the material is crossed over more tightly, and a deep, well-fitting belt of blue taffetas finishes the waist. The sleeves are full, and gathered dightly down the seam to give the rucked appearance. They reach to the elbow, and are finished with a band of broderie and frills of white pleated lawn. The skirt is simply made, being gathered in at the waist, and trimmed at the hem with a band of broderie and three full frills.
LADY CHELMSFORD.

Lady Chelmsford, whose husband has just been sppointed Governor of Queensland, is a daughter of Lord and Lady Wiinborne, and her eldest boy is now about nine years old. Lady Chelmsford last :-nry charming woman, and will make a most popular Governor's wife in Queensland, for she is in excellent hostess, and has inherited much of her mother's geniality and charm of manner.
CHAPTER XXIX, THE MYSTERY OF THE PAJARITO.

"His life must be saved at any cost," said Jordison, as they tried to revive the exhausted man. "I have made a mistake—a terrible mistake. Why the hell doesn't that fire burn up.? _Pour some oil on it."

-And all through that night the two men laboured with food and hot water, and brandy and warm blankets, Lipp, understanding nothing of what was going on, cursed in- cessantly, but a glance at his master's grim and terrible face told him that he must labour till their task was accomplished. At six o'clock in the morning Arthur Holme slept, and the light of life had crept once more into his ashen face. Twelve hours later he woke into conscious- ness. His wrists and ankles were lightly chained by pieces of rope, for Jordison knew that if ever he was to arrive at the truth, and conceal his own secret, he would have to play his part up to the end. In'spite of his bonds, Holme felt warm and comfortable, and shortly after he woke, Jordison fed him with some thick and steaming soup. The young man took it without a word. When he lad finished he looked at Jordison with question- ing eyes. " Yes," said Jordison sternly, " you've, guessed right. I want some information out of you, and dead men cannot speak. That soup is good, Lisn't it ? Well, there's lots. more of it. Bu 4 you go back to the tunnel, it you don't speak this time, and stay there till you rot. Do you understand ? " Holme nodded.

"If you tell me the truth," Jordison con- tinued, "I'll be merciful; I'll shoot you and spare you much suffering, and I 1 let Lady Agnes go free. Lipp, you can go."' The servant left the cavern, Holme pondered the matter for a minute, and then smiled. If he had to die it was better to die in comfort than face the slow starvation and darkness of the tunnel. Besides, Lady. Agnes's life would be saved. And the cer- tainty of that was worth all that he could give —even the minute chance of his own escape. "I'll speak," he said curtly. " I will tell you who I am. You said you were a friend of my father. I am Arthur Sterious, and I killed Richard Behag." Jordison rose to his feet. "You lie," he cried. I know well enough who you are. You are Richard Behag, and you killed Arthur Sterious."

Holme made no reply to Jordison's words. They had been flung at him as a thunder bolt is flung from the skies. The noise and crash of them was still in his ears. He was too stunned to make any answer. Nrp4L " Inrdison continued sternly, "you are Richard Behag, and it was the body of Arthur Sterious that was found on the shores north of Valparaiso. He was murdered." Still Holme did not speak. He clenched his bound hands and bowed his head. Jordi- son took out his watch and looked at it. _ _

"In half an hour's time," he said quietly, "you will be a dead man. But if you will tell me the truth, and all the tiath, I will release Lady Agnes Cliffe. If you refuse to speak, she shall die, too. I will give you two minutes to decide."

" Why do .you want to know ? " Holme replied, still not looking up from the ground; "of what interest is it to you? Who are you, and how does the death of either Behag or Sterious concern you ? " "It does not matter who I am," Jordison replied, "I have made you an offer, and you can take it or leave it. You have but a short time to consider the matter, and I should advise you not to waste it in conversation." Jordison spoke calmly, but every nerve and fibre of his being tingled with excitement. He was playing a gigantic game of bluff. What- ever reply came from Holme's lips, the lives of both Holme and Lady Agnes Cliffe were sale. Jordison could not kill either his own son or the woman that his son loved. But the wretched man yearned for some word that would free his son from the cloud that hung over his head—the murder of a companion, the robbery of a firm that had placed their trust in him: If he held out the hope of life, it was possible that Holme would not speak the truth. But a man on the verge of death will not lie when he knows that no words can save his life. If only Jordison could' have revealtd himself it would have been easy to arrive at the truth. But the man, for all his vileness, ha 4 one clear idea of honour in his mind—that the son must never know the terrible history of the father's life. He sat silent with the watch in his hal.d.

" The two minutes are up," he said at last. If Home had only looked at his faca he might have read the truth, he might have seen that the man was waiting anxiously, not for a confession of crime, but for a proof of inno- cence. But Iloliiie did not look up from the ground. However, the bribe was too great. Lady Agnes's life had to be saved at any cost. Jordison's bluff came oft successfully. " I will tell you all," the young man said, "but first you must swear by all you hold sacred—if indeed you hold anything sacred in heaven or earth—that Lady Agries chile shall return unmolested to her home."

"I swear this to you," Jordison said, earnestly. Holme looked him in the face and saw that the man was speaking the truth. "When I reached Valparaiso," he began, lordison interrupted him. "I should like you to start your story before that date. Why did you leave England ? " Holme paused for a moment. "Surely you don't want to know that ? " he said after a while.

" I do," Jordison answered. " I knew your father and mother, and you, too as a little t;hild. They were good folk. Why did you run away from them ? " He had a horrible fear that this part of the young man's story might disclose some fresh disgrace, some new evidence of the criminal instinct that had descended from father to son. His researches had failed to discover anything of the sort, but there are many sins which never come to light. "Well," Holme replied, after another pause, "if you insist, I must tell you. But I cannot think of it without shame now that my father and mother are both dead." Again he stopped, and a look of pair. crossed his face. "Go on," Jordison said, sternly, "look on me as your confessor. My lips are sealed."
Hohne shuddered. The 'reference to con- fession brought the idea of death very close to him.

"It is a simple story," be said hoarsely, "and a commonplace story. I was young, headstrong, and passionately fond of the sea. My parents—may God rest their souls— thought the life unfitted for a lad of promise and intellect. My father, whose whole heart was in his work, thought that. my life should be given to the propagation of Christianity in foreign parts. My heart did not fail ins at the • thought of the work, in fact, its dangers pro- vided the only bright spot in the life it offered. But—,Well, they say the sons of clergymen are often inclined to be irreligious. I understand it now. The perpetual air of piety was galling '.to me. I felt like the girl behind the coun te of the sweet shop, who could not ibear the taste of a single chocolate or caramel. The life had begun to stifle me. The air of the vicarage seemed close, narrow, and stuffy. The good side of it became more and more obscured. The disadvantages became more and more apparent. I was overwhelmed with the sanctity of it all. I longed to be free, to mingle with rough worldly folk, to say whatever I pleased, to do whatever I pleased. I was, of course, entirely in the wrong, but— perhaps you can understand." " I understand," Jordison replied. " Well, one morning I disappeared with a iew pounds in my pocket—the result of years of enforced thrift, set aside in a money box— and concealed myself in the labyrinth oat London. I got a job on a small merchant vessel and----" "That'll do," Jordison broke in. "Go or to Valparaiso." His heart yearned for even;

zrom his mind, The boy had not lett home re escape from the consequences of any disgracb- ,ful action. It was possible that the death of Arthur Sterious might yet be explained Jordison could not wait for details. "That was two years afterwards," said Holme; "my sixth voyage. How much de you know ? " Jordison told him briefly what the enquiry agent had discovered. "Well," said Holme, "I will now tell y'bu the truth. It would not save my neck in the dock, but it is the truth for all that. I have no reason to tell you a lie. I am not a criminal lying for his life." "I shall believe you," 'Jordison said, hurriedly, "go on with the story." "Well," Holme said, "one Sunday morn- ing Arthur Sterious and 1. went out f9r a sail in his boat, the ' Pajarito.' "

" The' robbery' first," cried Jordison, "tell me of that. I know nothing of that." Holme looked up at, him in surprise, and laughed bitterly. "Your interruption is excusable,", he said, slowly, "but I knew nothing of the robbery until after I was on the boat. Please let me tell my story in my own way." Jordison mumbled an apology. His heart was too full for words. He could have risen and clasped his son in his arms. But he only turned away his face, lest the younk man should see the joy that flared up in his eyes. "Well," Holme continued, "as I was say- ing, one Sunday morning we went out for a sail in the ' Pajarito.' We usually spent our Sundays on the water, sometimes in the large boat, but more often in the small one. Occasionally we did not return till daybreak on Monday morning. The boat contained two small but convenient berths, and a supply of water, biscnits,and tinned meat, was always kept on board. A yachtsman has to be prepared for emergencies. The mere drop- ping of the wind may--" "Yes, yes," Jordison interrupted im- patiently; "but go on with your story." "I mentioned the food," Holme continued with a slight frown, " because it Was through a casual inspection of our supplies that my suspicion of Sterious was first aroused. We were at the time some twenty miles out of ValParaiso, running before a fair breeze off the land., Sterious was at the tiller, and I went down into our little box of a cabin to get a drink of water. You can imagine* my surprise on opening the locker, where we kept our jar; to find a dozen bottles of whisky laying up against it. I opened the other lockers and found them crammed With food of every description. I also found four more large jars of water in the fore cabin. "I went up on deck and questioned Sterious. I think I asked him in jest if we were bound for Australia. He kept his eye on the burgee at our mast head, and replied that if I distracted his attention with silly ques- tion?, hp would certainly gybe the boat. "I said nothing more for a few minutes, but I lay on the deck and glanced at his face front time to time, and 'noticed 'a curious look on it. He kept his eyes fixed on ithe little fluttering flag as though all his wits were needed to steer by it. But I knew that this excessive care was quite unnecessary, and as I puffed thoughtfully at my pipe, I turned the matter over in my mind, and to say the truth, began to be a little uneasy about it. I offered to take the tilkr, but he curtly refused, and still kept the boat's head into the west.

" After a time I repeated my•question, and he looked at me thoughtfully, as though try- ing to gauge my interest in the matter. Then he made a clean breast of the whole affair. He spoke hastily, as though half ashamed of his words, but yet with an air of dogged deter- mination ,that argued ill for any opposition on my part. "lie explained that he had stolen the keys of the safe, one from me and one from his father, and that he had on board at that minute ,e,s,ciob in cash and £595,000 worth of negotiable securities. He went on to say that he would have taken me earlier into his con- fidence, but that he had some doubts of my Loyalty--I think that was the word he used. I thanked him in my heart for these doubts, and I saw at once the true reason of his friendship. I was at the time sorry, for I had a real liking for Sterious, in spite of all his vices. I did not •then know to what depths a desperate man :an sink, though I knew a few hours after- wards.

"He went on to say that we were pro- visioned for a month, and that our destination was Iquiqui. He laboriously explained as though defending himself, that he had chosen tins means of escape for good reasons. He intended that the' Pajarito should never be seen again, and that we should both be ac- counted dead men.

"He concluded by generously offering to go haves with me, if I would assist him in his sc3eme. I will do the man justice on this point. He could have made away with me, and ensured my silence effectually, but it was not till I had driven him in a corner that he attempted my life. "He rounded off the effectiveness of his ipeech by casually producing a revolver and dipping it back into his pocket again. I was ten feet from him at the time, or I would hyve tried to take it from him before we started the liscussion on the matter.

"I replied, as I think most men of my ;tamp would have done. I thanked him sar- castically for considering me in the matter. I cviled lima in Language that only a sailor could have conceived. I expostulated with him, and tried to work on his better feelings as a gentleman, and the son of an honourable man. I panted out to him the ruin he would orttig on ins father's firm, I exhausted every means in my power, But ho was hard as steel and I could not even scratch the surface of his mind. I concluded by stating emphatically that I meant, to bring the Pajarito ' into Valparaiso that night, and save ,him from the consequences of his folly. "We thrashed the matter out for two hours I _

and he backed up his arguments with his piPtol. I shall not forget those hours as long as I live. I can still see the blue, glorious sky, the (lancing waves, the white swelling sails, the man at the stern, one hand on the tiller and one on his revolver, and above all the deepening lines of evil on the handsome face. 'ln the end we compromised: He agree' d to let me drop out of the business. He said he would put use ashore at a small village fifty miles north of Valparaiso, a place outside all railways and telegraph wires, and that he would go through with the affair by himself. I swore to use no force to turn him from his purpose, and we resumed our relations at fellow yachtsmen on a boat that required the attention of both of us.

" After lunch I felt drowsy, and fell asleep. When I woke up I was lying on the deck with my face to the sky, and I was bound hand and foot. Steriou3 was at the tiller, and I noticed with surprise that he had my clothes on. I saw my ring on his finger, and a gold Mexican coin which had been given me by one of the men on the ' Valetta ' dangled from my watch chain on my waistcoat. I glanced at my own body. He had transferred all his own things to me. I was dressed in his clothes, and his rings were on my fingers. I could even feel something strang& about my shirt and underclothing. It .was evident that he had drugged me and changed every single article of my attire. His motives were un- pleasantly clear. So long as I was alive this mere change of habiliments could be of no value to him, but my body, washed up some weas hence on the coast, unrecognisable save for the garments, rings, etc., would be an adequate proof of the death of Arthur Sterious. :Before I spoke, I carefully examined his face. A great change had come over it during the last few hours. All the evil seemed to have worked up to the surface. It had always been dissolute, but now it had become criminal..

" I will not detail to you the conversation that ensued, and which lasted for over an hour. Sterious made it quite clear to me that he in- tended to kill me. He also confessed that he had been too much of a coward to kill me in cold blood, While I was unconscious, He sug- ,e,ded that I should have a fight for my life out expiained that it would have to be a rigtii where I was bound to lose the day—the fight of an unarmed man against one armed with a revolver. lli•inked him for his considera• tion and accepted the chance in the spirit it •,vhich it '•\'as ''fferell• He was at least as muct of a sportsman as the man who fights a part. ridve with a double barrelled gm,

LANCASHIRE JUNIOR CUP DRAW.

A meeting of the Lancashire County Rugby Union was held at the Grosvenor Hotel, Manchester on Tues- day evening, Mr. F. W. Wright presiding. The follow- ing clubs were admitted to membership :—Salford St. John's, Runcorn Fertilisers,Runcorn nightield, Runcorn Juniors, and Castner-Kellner. The draw lor the first round of the Lancashire Junior Cup, to be played on October 21, on the ground of the clubs first named, resulted as follows :—Rocbdale Rangers v. Hey Side ; Rochdale Athletics v. Hollin- wood ; Neville Hornets v. Radcliffe Rangers; Runcorn Juniors v. Runcorn Fertilisers ; Walker's Brewery v. Runcorn Highfield ; Widnes Rangers v. Castner-Kellner; West Legh v. Leigh Shanirocks; Tyldesley v. Highfield (Wigan); Pemberton v. Leigh Rangers ; Prestwich Church v. General Electric ; Salford St. Bartholomew's v. Egerton ; Barrow Marsh Hornets v. Pennington United ; Barrow St. George's v. Dalton ; Ulverstone Rangers v. Salford; and St. John's and Ice, byes.

div.head: PENNY GULLIVER.
div.p: THE PENNY GULLIVER.

The story of Lemuel Gulliver's adventures amongst the Brobdingnagians, as well as amongst the Lillipu- tians, will always, we hope, continue to be as popular with the youth of this country as it has been ever since Dean Swift issued it to the public of his day as a counterblast to the "Travellers Tales" of needy adven- turers, who found a publisher for " adventures of the mind" which served to keep in disrepute, until our own day, the works of Marco Polo and Bakluyt. The parody on the works referred to served its purpose, but "Gulliver's Travels" will, all the same, always live as a fairy tale. Messrs. Newnes' edition at a penny is a marvel of cheapness—sixty-four pages, half the size of "Tit-Bits" The other volumes of Messrs. Nevvne's penny Library, good as they are, are, we understand, to he much improved upon in the near future. Even now, however, they are about good enough for most people at the

div.head: EMPiRE 00IFFEIRE.
div.p: THE EMPiRE 00IFFEIRE.

A great effort has been made this season to revive the old Empire style of hair-dressing, and many a pretty maiden has been seen with her hair drawn upwards, a mass of little curls forming the Porn- 7adour pouf. With one of these coiffures was worn s wide band of diamonds; but prettiest of all for young girl is an Empire wreath—diamonds will ioubtless come later. White or coloured tulle threaded through the hair is still a favourite head- iress, but it is not always becoming, and, if not very carefully arranged, in dark hair it sometimes ;ives the idea of there being a grey lock among the darker tresses.

div.head: TIPS "BEAUTY STORES."
div.p: TIPS "BEAUTY STORES."

The nowest development, says a writer in Truth, LS a "Beauty Stores." The most ill-favoured woman —provided she ha.; sufficient money—may enter one pf these establishments, and be fitted out as a store- Venus. Golden hair is fixed on her skull, thick syebrows and lashes are added to her face, the trimmest and whitest teeth are placed in her mouth, her complexion is coloured to her taste, ner skin is rendered smooth, her figure is arti- -scially built up, and upon this scaffolding is arranged a becoming dress and costume. "Beauty " may be had at almost all prices, beginning from £10! GIRL'S COAT.

The little girl's coat shown in the sketch could be carried out with equal success in serge, cloth, or linen; but perhaps for present wear it would be particularly charming carried out in dark green linen, worn with a prettily-shaped collar of white spotted muslin, bordered with a

rather heavy insertion. The coat is arranged in box-pleats, and is slightly shaped to the figure at the sides. The wide box-pleat or panel down the front is made separately, and attached to t'io coat. It it cut in a V at the neck, and is trimmed with linen-covered buttons. Large buttonholes are made on each side of the pleats, and a belt of the same linen passed through. The sleeves are a small bishop shape, which will generally be found the most becoming for children's garments.

div.head: WOODEN BUTTONS.
div.p: WOODEN BUTTONS.

Wooden buttons are to decorate our winter gowns, and some of these will be very prettily carved or pokered." Many of our home wood carvers are giving their spare time during the holidays to preparing sets of buttons for their autumn dresses.

div.head: " DUFFER " SCULLING CONTEST.
div.p: A " DUFFER " SCULLING CONTEST.

At a recent river garden-party sculling com- petitions for girls, on a quiet backwater, pro- vided amusement for the whole afternoon. Lots were d:awn for the heats, and even those who bad no knowledge of rowing were pressed into service, one man being allowed to each crew. The attempt of " stroke " to keep his crew in some sort of order was perhaps more amusing t.) those on the bank than to the agitated damsels themselves, whose well-meant attempts to free the nose of the boat from the starting place among the rushes frequently ended in catching crabs," and an inextricable confusion of oars and boat-hooks. Prizes were given to those whose scratch crew chewed most energy, as well as to the winners in the different heats.

"He loosed my hands ana sprang nacx co the tiller. I unfastened the rest of the ropes myself, and took cover behind the mast.. He fired once and splintered the wood by my face. But before he could fire again, the wind sud- denly shifted, and the boat gybed. He hauled at the main sheet with one hand, but was too late. The boom came flying across, and he had only just time to duck his head. The heavy spar caught his hand and sent the S revolver spinning into the water, We were once more on equal terms. "I Auggested a truce, but he would have none of it, and wrenching out the iron tiller from the rudder, he came at me. As luck would have it, the spare tiller, which was larger than the one in ordinary use, and reser- ved for dirty weather, lay up against the fore combings. Before he could reach me I was ready to meet him, " Every detail of that fight, which lasted for over ten minutes, is still vivid in my mind. I will only tell you, however, that in the end I broke through his guard with a terrific blow, and the square end of my tiller crashed into his skull. He died without a sound or a word, _ .

" At first I resolved to return to Valparaiso and tell the whole story to the authorities. But on second thoughts I saw the inherent improbability of the tale. It would certainly have been believed, as indeed your detective gathered from the police, that we had both made off with the securities, and quarrelled over the division of the spoil. Moreover, justice in South America and in England are two different things. Sterious was the son of a wealthy man, and I had no doubt his father's position would influence the judge in his decision.

"To cut a long story short, T sailed the boat northwards to within five mil* of a desolate shore, took the securities from Sterious's pocket and the cash from the locker where he had placed it, and threw the body overboard., I left the clothes, etc., as Sterious himself had arranged them. I had now similar reasons for preserving my secret, INvished the world to think that Richard I3ehag was dead. . _ . . . .

"That night I scuttled the ' Pajarito ' in fifty fathoms of water, and rowed ashore in the dinghy. I subsequently made my way to Iquiqui, and took the first ship to England. "On my arrival I posted all the stolen property to its lawful owners, only keeping back two thousand pounds for my own use. This was almost the precise amount that I had to my credit in Valparaiso, as the result of a lucky speculation in wheat, and which I knew would be confiscated. It is odd that the police did not seize upon this clue, and arrive at the true facts.

"Of my doings in England it is sufficient to say that I have worked hard, and trebled my money in four years. I have since tried to lead a more intellectual and a better life, and my plans for the future—" He stopped suddenly. He remembered that his plans for the future had been arranged for by Jordison. "Is there anything more you want to know? "he broke out fiercely and sullenly. "Nothing," replied Jordison, faintly. "EZ you believe what you have already heard ? '

"I believe you," the man replied. Then he buried his face in his hands, and his whole frame trembled with emotion—with joy at his son's innocence, with agony at the blood- stained record of his own life, And there, in the quiet depths of the earth, he silently vowed once more to keep a knowledge of his identity from his son, and prayed ' that he might have the strength to keep his vow to the end.

A SIMPLE BOILER PACKING.

Writing to the S ientific American on the subject of packing for boiler manholes, an Indiana corre- spondent says: I would like to offer one, which for cheapness and simplicity I believe 'hard to beat, Take three pieces of strawboard—more often called pasteboard—about gin. thick, each piece about 3,n. larger than the manhole. Glue these together, making gin. thick altogether, then with pattern of manhole (this pattern with about lin. rim can be sawn out of a thin board and kept for future use) mark the strawboard when dry, and saw out with scroll saw. This packing will not shrink and split open like those made of wood. I have seen it used successfully for nearly two years. An old boilermaker, who is now boiler inspector for this part of the State, told me it was new to him, con- sequently it must be new to a great many.
A RUBBER FILM GLOVE.

A rubber film glove, the feature of which is its ant septic qualities, has been devised for surgeons. The idea consists of immersing the hands in a weak solution of gutta-percha in benzine or acetone, or applying the solution to the skin of the patient. The purpose of the film is to seal the surfaces of either the hands or skin with an insoluble, im- pervious, and practically imperceptible pellicle, which will not allow the secretions of the skin to escape, and will not admit blood, pus, or secretions into the crevices of the skin. Such a protective measure for surgpons is preferable to working with rubber gloves, inasmuch as the sense of touch or pliability of the skin is not impaired in any way, as is the case when detachable gloves are used.

div.head: PROBLEM OF THE NIAGARA FALLS.
div.p: PROBLEM OF THE NIAGARA FALLS.

Among Scientific circles considerable interest has been taken in the question of the probable time it has taken Niagara Falls to make the gorge, and further the time it will likely take to wear through to Lake Erie. Professor Maury has gone deep into the study of this problem, having followed the theories advanced by Sir Charles Lyell. In an address he quotes Sir Charles as estimating the time required to cut the seven-mile gorge at about 38,000 years. The first survey was made in 1842, when the exact position of the falls was mapped. Several surveys since then have been made, the last being in 1890. The average yearly recession for the American Falls is sixty-four hundredths of a foot, and that of the Horseshoe 2ft. 18in. Thus it may be assumed that the mean recession of a cataract combining the volume of both falls, "such as," he declares, "existed throughout most of the period of excabation, would be at least 3ft. a year, and perhaps as much as 4ft. or sft."

CAN EXTINCT SPECIES BE RESUSCITATED? Professor Standf us, of Zurich, Switzerland, has succeeded in developing practically new species, as well as in reviving some very ancient species, by developing caterpillars into butterflies under certain conditions of temperature. Be took 6,000 cater- pillttri and exposed them to temperatures ranging from 25deg. to 99deg. Fahrenheitt and thus pro- duced butterflies which are ordinarly found in districts as far separated as the Arctic and the Torrid Zones, and others of species which have been extinct for a long time. Still more remark- able were new specks, never before heard of, tinted all the colours of the rainbow, which are practically priceless to the rich collet:. Pro- fessor Standfus thinks he will be able to produce equally wonderful results from other forms of life in the bird and animal world.

The workmen in the quicksilver mines, and, to a less extent, those engaged in the manufacture of barometers and other instruments in which mercury is used, are liable to suffer from a peculiar form of poisoning produced by continually breathing mercury vapour. The disease, which is known as "the trembles," or "mercurial tremor," affects the nervous system, so that the sufferer is attacked by fits of trembling whenever any attempt is made to use the muscles, and it eventually ends in death. In the mines in Spain. Austria, and America it is usual to remove workmen to other parts of the works comparatively free from the vapour so soon as they shew the characteristic signs of poisoning; hut the Spaniards in South America did not pay Oven this amount of attention to their miners. A mining community was founded towards the close of the sixteenth century at nuancavelica, in Peru, to work the celebrated mine of St. Barbara, in which is a subterrinean village with a church cut out of the cinnabar. This mine was a great source,of profit to the Spanish, and it is estimated that during their rule thousands of the lncliAns driven to work there died of mercury poisoning. No serious attempt appears to have been made to grapple with this evil except that in certain mines Letter systems of ventilation have been adopted, and it has been left to an Italian chemist to devise ,sitnple means of prevention. Dr. Tarugi has found that aluminium in a finely.divided state im- mediately absorbs mercury even when only traces of the metal are present in a large volume of air. The amalgam produced is very stable, and can be heated to 200 deg. 0., or twice the temperature of boiling water, without losing the slightest trace of mercury. This absorptive power of aluminium is so great that the reaction can be used as an extremely sensitive test for mercury. ln order to utilise this property of aluminium in the prevention of mercury poisoning, Dr. Tarugi ha S devised a respirator containing several layers of very fine aluminium gauze. which will allow the air to nass *must ietaming every trace or mercury vapour. ; This respirator will probably before long be adopted in all quicksilver mines."—Knoteledo.

Let me own up at once that I had gone into that room *here the eouspirators had their trial, for nothing more or less than a common burglary. It is a horrible thing fur a man in a position like mine then was to have to confess, but I may as well make a clean breast of the truth. I had been heavily dipped for over two years ; It had taken all the cleverness I could think of to keep in the regiment ; and a bad Doncaster week and then a regular crashing bad night at . Poker put the lid on my professional cofflu for • once and always. I had no choice but to send in 1"Y papers, and I came up to -town to try and think out what must come next. It was the glint of that woman'e diamonds iii the hotel dining. room which gave me the hint md although the bare idea of the thing made me shiver with cold at first, the more I thought of it, the more it seemed that there was no other road out of the • mod. Now never mind which hotel all this happened -111 ' • it was one of the big ones in Northumber- land Avenue ; and there were some two hundred 'Teeple, all well-dressed, chatteriug away in the ,dining-room. The weinan with the diamonds 'was at the next table, with her back to me. She was wearing a gown that I'll swear hadn't been out of Paris a week. She'd dark red Lair, small •ears, and as fine a neck as one could wish to bee. And on her neck and in her hair, she'd great white glittering gems which made my mouth - dry with longing when I looked at them. I -knew that there must have been ten or twelve 'thousand sovereigns sunk in those stones. I was a judge of jewellery then : heaven knows I had bought enough of it for one woman and another since I had left Sandhurst. I looked off and on at the back of that neck :ma hair in a dazed sort of way for quite ten 'nitrides, and then an idea jumped into my heed wlnch made me sigh and turn away. But tho impudent glitter of the necklace and the stars •drew roe back, and presently I found myself Pushing the claret aside arid ordering a small bottle of 'B4 Krug. As we sat, she was not a yard away : and every time she moved, the scent front her hair and her dress came to ate in tiny waves. Once she turned half round to look .down the room. She was deliciously beautiful. I -guessed her age as rising twenty-throe. She was dining with two men, and the trio •of them spoke Freuch ; but though they rattled out Parisian argot with easy fluency, I could see that the language was not their native tongue. After a while I grasped the fact that they were itil three Russians. The man with the torpede beard was named Parloff, ana apparently served in the navy ; and the clean-shaved fellow with the high pitched voice was Dimitri something or •other. Dimilri seemed by his manner to be a gentleman. He called the lady in the diamonds " Sonia," and they appeared to be on terms of easy familiarity. But Parloff addressed her as " Countess," and seemed instinctively to take the role of social inferior, whether he wished to or not. It was to the vague Dimitri I owed the hint which turned me from a mere spectator who could covet, into the active-fingered bur- "By the way," I heard him say, that isn't Taste, Sonia. which you're wearing to-night I suppose 1•" " You are paying a very poor compliment to 'Thy diamonds." " 31a el/Pre, you are next them, and you always .outshine mere jewellery." " Pouf !" she said, " how broad ! You must 'nave been practising your compliments on Eng- lish barmaids during these last weeks since you've been in London." " Alt !" he answered, " I've been in queer 'company since I saw you last, Sonia. Our ex- celletit friends here are more noted for their earuestness than their polish. And moreover they are few of them affluent. It would be rather
to-iiiunt those stones before. them."

"Oh Dimitri " she said, " how dreadfully 'thoughtless of me ! Poor fellows, I know how bard-up some of them must be." "And the passage down to the—er—to our 1/".loe of entertainment to-night is quite dark," "Rttl Dimitri, "and it would be a pity to tempt ar!u_canaille to steal."

1 - "Do not call any of our friends canaille, " ', 'MA the man with the torpedo beard. "The .Cause makes us all equal." " Theoretically,' said Dimitri with a laugh. " But heaven forbid that we should become so Practically, in the details of dress and dinners, fur instance. I much prefer that those should remain dealt out as they are already. But Par. off quite right about your more moveable orna- ments. Shall we go out and have our coffee in the hail? These barbarous English object to our smoking a cigarette in the room where we eat." You oetter coffee and your petits verses," said the Countess, " and I'll go up to Number Forty. :me and take off these diamonds, and be with you itt a couple of minutes. I suppose we needn'l leave the hotel for another hour yet I' —" She ,ISlanced up at the clock— "It is twelve min "tem to nine now, and we are not due there till ten.', Dirrikri rose to his feet and picked up her fan. ," It's quite half an hour's drive. We must leave here by nine-thirty. The business will be twer by . . And that was all I heard. The chatter of the Rreat room drowned the rest of. his word.', and I "tared after them stupidly till they had passed Out of the room and a bowing waiter had let the 14 tying doors close noiselessly upon Parloff's , "eels. " I crilered another small bottle of champagne, held a hissing goblet in the grip of my hand . ' "tlt I did not drink. My mind was in a boil. I was arguing with myself how a man would feel f:vhen he had chucked even the rudiments ot "onour to the winds, and become a common Vlferer and thief. I . limed awl began to walk across the flour, but at the end of the first step I halted and a thing hap- ened which turned all ray blood to ice. I heard Me outer dour ot Ulu z•ilt •uiu Dinatri's voce say " Go in first, Sonia, and receive them." _ _ _

If fill means had bz..en at hand, I would have killed myself at that tumneut to have got away from what appeared to be my certain shame. But I was empty-handed, and helpless, and I stood in the darlmess of that bed-room like a man dazed, and looked OIL through the slit of the door- way. There were tett men with the Countess in the other room. The two I had seen before and two others were in evening dress the rest wore ordinary black and tweed, with that sonic- thing indefinable in the cut which marks elf the foreigner. The chatter of their voices rang through my head for full ten minutes without leaving any impression, and then someone rapped a table for silence and spoke. " Friends ' lie said " our ally here, who is in the British Parliament on our baalf, under- stands no Russian. He has come to-night to see justice done, and it is right tin:t he should ;if:pm:bite everything that happens. So if it please you, we will conduct our proceedings in French."

- The assembly chattered out its cordial con- sent, and the Englishman thanked them. His accent was vile, but his French was glib enough. Parka went on : " I was sorry to drag you away so unceremouiowdy front our other meet- ing, but necessity knows no etiquette. News was brought me that treachery had been done to our Cause. Our plans for—you know what —have been betrayed. The whole scheme is totally split for the present. And I make to doubt that more of our friends in Petersburg are at this moment marching oil towards Sigh:diem The Czar's gold," be added bitterly " has once more saved his imperial hide." " I'm beginning to admire the Czar." said " His hand is everywhere. He is a man worth fighting against." Falloff frowned and waved him to silence. " The traitor is growing alarmed already. He fears the reach of our arm here in London, and has made arrangements to return to Petersburg to-inorrow. But before he goes be has promised to call at this hotel to make his adieux to the Countess, end perhaps we may induce him not to folget the ceremony " He drew from his pocket a sheaf of papers and pitched them on the table. The English M.P. and the other man in evening dress took them up to examine-- "Thieve are written proofs of the man's treachery, and again we have to Manic the Countess here for putting them into our hands and directing vengeance to the right man. It only remains then to fix upon his sentence." "Oh death, I suppose," said a man with a pock-marked face, " There is no reason for de- viating from our general rule that I can sea ?" " Except," said Parlotf, " the difficulty of carrying it out. I make no doubt that our caller will have a couple of detectives waiting outside in Northumberland Avenue tUI he shall have finished his call. We are all more or less known to them, and if our man is not forthcoming again in this life, it will go bard with us. We can't afford to sacrifice ourselves for a case like this ; the Cause has .more work for us to do ; and we must exact our penalty, and at the same time keep ourselves safe. But I have brought this with me," lie said, " from the club," and turned round, and drew from the pocket of his overcoat which lay on a chair, a short handled whip with two metal rings in the lash, and a beak-like hook It its end.

Dimitri frowned. "Oh I say," he protested, " to knout the man is worse than killing him." " Precisely," said Parloff, and looked at his watch. "He has earned the hardest punish- ment we can give. Think of the misery he has mused to his associates. Think of the poor wretches now tramping towards Asia and exile. And now friends, please, get ready for this traitor's reception. He named his time, and he will be punctual. He may drop in upon us any minute. We must cease talking, or our voices will scare luni. He thinks that there is no one here but the Countess." The men settled themselves on to their seats and forebore even to whisper. The Countess leaned with one white elbow on the mantlepieee looking into the fire and biting her lips. The English M.P. went methodically through the sheaf of papers. For myself I stood in a dull agony where I was. I had crept over to the outer door of the bed-room and found it locked, and it seemed that my detection was only a mat- ter of time. . .

..... The minutes dragged on with a horrible slow- ness. It appeared to me that hours passed, and I made certain that the man who was expected had got wind of what awaited him, and was stay- ing under snug protection elsewhere. And I think some of the Nihilists had gathered the same notion, for they began to get restless and to throw glances of enquiry across at Parloff. But he always nodded back with confidence, and t last a sharp knock rattled on the panels in the door.

Parloff got up, drew a knife from its sheaf at his back and turned the handle himself. The Countess from over by the fireplace said " Come in." The door opened, and a tall young fellow stepped into the room with a smile on his face which froze there when he saw who were waiting for him. He tried to retreat, but Parloff had closed and locked the door, and stood on guard with his weapon raised : so he thrust his hands into his trousers pockets and looked coolly round him. . .
But meanwhile the Countess was staring at him with a face of horror. " You " she burst out at last, " you! Why have you come hereP"

" Because you sent for me to make my adieux." " I did no such thing. Colonel Bieue, believe me, I expected someone else. You had better go." The newcomer looked relieved. "I am in the way it appears. Well, Countess, let it be au teroir, and not adieu. I suppose we shall meet next, week in Petersburg.—Captain Parloff, I'll trouble you for the key of the door." " You shall have it after our business is done" il Parka. " But for the present we shall ask you to stay with us until some formalities have keen gone through—Ali "—of a sudden the man had been seized from behind, gagged, and thrown to the ground. The Countess came forward, her face as white 'IV paper, her hands stretched out convulsively. Monsieur Parloff " she said, " Dimitri, Mes. sieurs. take care what you do. This is not the Welt I expected. He has not betrayed our Cause, it is some other. . . ." . .

The English M.P. at the table looked up. " Par- don me, Madame," he said, " but you are mis- hd(en. The proofs are here amongst these pap. us, in black and white. There is unfortunately no doubt about the matter." " But Colonel Biene is my friend." " There is no room " said the Englishman " for private sentiment in a question like this. If fruiters were not weeded out, the Cause would break up in a week." Parlotf rapped for silence. " Time is passing," he said, "we have little to waste. The knout has been I,cided on : I think sixty lashes will suffice."

"My God," cried the Countess, " sixty will kill any man.'' " Not a soldier of Colonel Biene's constitu- tion " said the man with the pock-marked face end he took up the whip and ran the thong with its rings through his fingers. "It has been my unfortunate duty to administer this punishment hefore, and for the sake of all who are here I will see that it does not kill. But in the next five minutes Colonel Diem) shall earn an experience that will last him for the rest of his life." The Countess sank into a chair, and buried her fee* in her The men who bad pinned Biene to the floor lifted him to 1114 feet and stripped eft the upper part of his dress. Then they reared is soya on end against the wall, and lashed hies to it v ropes from the wrists and ankles. Then they eloed aside, the pock-marked man with the knout took up his position. and Parloff addressed the prisoner. tt Celonel lfiette," he sad, " the plan of cam- paigo which this Society of ours has made against the Czar of the P,ussitis has \teen entirely frus- trated by the malignant treach:ry of one ut our members. Not only has the eretUt of our cause two's damaged, but the severity 'he Russian pike I OWSI rdB or sympathisers !lac been im s - mssply inerett,e To you all this is owing, and by the r,th,;., of our association, which you Ca- to t.hur. full when you first betattne a mem. Again the prisoner shook his head in denial. " Very well," said. Parloff, " then, for your obstinacy, I add ten more lashes to your sentence, making it now seventy in all—you may begin." The Dock-marked man stewed back and mea• surett the distance in nis eye. Then ne up his arm and sent the ringed lash of the knout whistling through the air. It fell on the bared muscles of Colonel Biene's shoulders with a sick- ening splash, but how he took the blow I could not see. The Countess had sprung across the room, and stood before WM.
" This must not iro on," she saio, panting. " That man is innocent "
" Madame, by these papers—" began the Englishman at the table....
" Pah, they are forged." " I am afraid we 3allllot accept that statement now as evidence."
" But I give you my word Colonel Biene is not guilty." " Then you can doubtless lay your hand on the culprit F" She looked round the room with wild eves.

" I could," she whispred. " You mean to say that someone else now here betrayed the plot to the Petersburg police ?" She hesitated and then nodded. " Then you will have the kindness to niention a name, and show your proofs." She hesitated again, and shuddered violently. She tried to speak, but could not. Then she slowly raised a forefinger and pointed to herself. Dimitri sprawr up, facing her. "My God, Sonia," he cried. " You ! Do you know what this means ? You must be dreaming I Sonia. you must be mad ! You cannot get Bien() off this way : they will knout you in his place." " I know what I am saying," she answered huskily, " and I know what it will cost. But I cannot help that now. I have earned it." Parlolf gave an order, and the prisoner was cast off from the whipping block and given his clothes. They removed the gag front his mouth but he spoke not a word. The room was hung in silence, but from outside there came the hum of London, dimmed by the windows. Only one appeal did the Countess make. " Oh," she said, " will you not have mercy on me because I am a woman ?" Bat Parlotf shock his head, and no one lifted a voice for mercy. The pock-marked man came across the floor, and laid it hand on the bodice of her dress. She shrank away front hint. " I know what you mean," she said, " but I will not have you touch me before it is necessary." And then be- fore ti em all she stripped off her upper gar- ments, and of her own accord went and stood against the up-ended sofa. The pock-marked man came up with the lashings and made her fast, knot by knot. A pink colour rose up under her ivory Ann which deepened as he worked. The fellow finished at last, picked up the knout and stepped back, looking up for orders. Parloff white to the lips sat in his chair without a word. No one spoke, no one moved, and the laboured breathing of the Countess fell clearly upon my ear where I stood behind the gap of the bedroom door.

The pock-markea man coughed. Parloft gave a deep sigh, nodded, shut his eyes, and sank his chin upon his chest. The pock-marked man straightened out the knout with his fingers, threw the lash behind his shoul- der, and then swung it with horrid force on to the comely bare back of the woman before him. The metal rings threw up spurts of blood from where they fell, the thongs almost buried themselves in the soft flesh, but the Countess uttered no sound. Her head drooped. She had fainted. Then a surprising thing happened. Colonel Biene shot out his fist, mid the pock-marked Mall flew backwards across half the room and lay on the carpet like a pole-axed bullock. Dimitri at the same moment jumped to his feet, awl I saw that there was a revolver in his hand.

" I can't stand thia," he cried. "It bas got to stop, and if there is any one who calls himself ii man here he will help me." The Englishmen jumped to his feet with shut fists. "By God, yes," he said. " I'm there too."

Parloff raised his head wearily. "Do you suppose I like it either ?" he asked. " But we arc not individuals hero. We are simply items in the machinery of the Cause. And it is our duty—" M.P.Tue interrupted him rudely. " The sacred Cause be damned," said he. " I lin cc endured most things for it; I have rubbed my shoulders with half the scum of Bit,mia for its sake ; I have got myself disliked by every decent man who knew inc here iii Englaiel and I have never grumbled till tiow."—fle wagged a fore- finger at the Countess' hack.—" Bat this is too much. Brutes who will do that to a W 0111,111: tlrell't fit to live, and there's my opinim of the lot of yon. Now wade in and murder toe if von like." No oile stirred.

" Very well," he said, and opened his pen- knife. " Now I am going to cut loose the ropos by which this lady is tied up, and then I shall ring for her maid. If any of you want to wait and give explanations, you C/111 du an, but for my- self I am sufficiently a,hatned to have a wish never to see this hotel or any of you again." lie turned to the upright sofa and began to haggle at the ropes with his knife. Ile other tacit in the ro•nn began hurriedly collecting their hats and cloaks. One by one they weut out into the passage, till the rank and file hail all de- parted ' • and then Parlotf went with the pock- marked loan on his arm ; and then Dimitri fol- lowed with Colonel Bien() ; till at last only the Englishman was left with his finger upon the bell-push. He was not two seconds hehind the others, and the Countess lay insett•ible on the floor as the only occupant of the room. At any moment the maid might come ; but till she arrived the place was empty of anyone who could interfere. With a thumping heart I darted across the floor and gaincd the corridor outside. The last of the Nihilists was jut turn- ing down towards the stair. I was a free man still, and a gush of joy should have filled me when I remembered that I had failed to become a thief. But ou my soul I could not help regretting those diamonds which had been left -behind. Indeed if the Countess had not proved herself so monstrous plucky, I am sure that I should have taken them.

But as it was, I have never seen either her or the jewels since, or even heard of them, because I made another attempt to re,,ruit my vanished funds that night, which compelled me to leave the hotel next morning without beat of drum.

A youth in a white apron is serving some I , customers outside, and you politely enquire after the cocker of the first cab. " Monsieur is at dinner, inside," is the reply. You look in, and see not only Monsieur, but other Measieurs, with glazed hats, red waistcoats, their coats off— etiquette demands this—enjoying their meal. If you are indiscreet enough to call one of them, Mosieur will first wink at you, then solemnly raise his glass, drink your health and continue his meal. Gentlemen's coach- men so wellas those of hired broughams, belong alto- gether to a different class. They are experienced men, ' capital drivers, but held in lofty contempt by the cocher 1 .de :arum The latter has even invented for them a , rather funny name, but which, like the rest of his voca- bulary, is unfit for publication.—" Tbe King." 1 THE FASCINATION OF TREASURE HUNTING I There is a fascination about the "human documents" : unfolded month by month in the "Wide World ; Magazine" which one finds in the contents of no other , publication. Take, for instance, "The Man in the ; Leather Waistcoat," in the August issue. This is a I sailor's plain tale of his voyage with a strange old man i who professed to bold tan secret of the Cocos Island I Treasure—a private hoard valued at many millions, for i which countless expeditions have searched in vain. The i old man's papers—here set forth for the first time— may be of great value or of none, but their possibilities I are fascinating to anyone who feels inclined to go I treasure hunting. Another stirring narrative is 1‘ The Fate of the Skidbv," being the appalling experi- ences of Captain J. H. Pearson, who was wrecked on I"the graveyard of the Atlantic." Lord Hindi ip describes his wanderings in Eastern Africa, ; and two other unique i journeya are dealt with in " Across the Great Snow Desert," and "Of! the Beaten Track in the Himalayas." The striking photographs occompanying all these articles bring home to the reader with telling realism I the scenes depicted. A topical article is "The Police 1 of Japan," giving much interesting information about the Japanese "man in blue," who is a wonderful bargain at five :billings a week, which is what a grateful i country pays him. No less than ten other articles and 1 stories, all of first-class interest, make lip a splendid ; number—the very thing for holiday reading. REPRISALS AFTER THE BATTLE OF CAMDEN. The war resumed its old character, but with embittered temper and added ferocity. Lord Cornwallis had been enraged to find among the prisoners both British deserters and militia who had broken their parole. He proclaimed that all militia who should join the enemy were to be hanged when caught, and that vigorous punishment should be meted out upon all who violated their allegiance. In prescribing these severities he was : only following the example of the Georgian legislature ! which in the previous year had hanged a hatch of ! loyalists for "treason." But reprisals were followed by 1 counter-reprisals, until a very inferno reigned in many ! parts of the Carolinas. It was civil war in its most odious shape, reproducing many of the savage features I of that Indian warfate with which the rude combatants lof either faction were well acquainted. Over and over I again in his despatches. Cornwallis complains of i "blood most wantonly and inhumanly shed under Ithe mock forms of justice," and of "the shocking tortures and inhuman murders which are every day committed by the enemy, not otly on those who have taken part with us, but on many who refuse to join them." " I must observe," he wrote on one occasion to an American general, "that the cruelty exercised on the prisoners taken under Ms)or Ferguson iis shocking to humanity, and the hanging poor old I Colonel Mills, who was always a fair and open enemy 'to your cause, was an act of most savage barbarity." But there was brutality enough and to spare among i those who wore the King's uniform. Andrew Jackson, I a lanky stripling of fourteen, was cruelly simile,: over wrist and head by an officer of the Legion whose boots he had declined to clean on the ground that he was a , prisoner of war. The scars he had carried with him to I the grave, and we may well fancy that they burned a ' deeper red that January morning when Pakenham's veterans were mown down like grass before the batteries of New Orleans.—From " Farleton in the Legion," in the " Cornhill Magazine" for August. CONCERNING OTHER FELLOWS. Writing on "Streakiness" in the "Windsor," the School-Boy says:—" Wainwright is the cleverest chap I know (bar one, whom it would not become me to mention); but his love of punning leads people not intimate with him to mistake him for a fool. However, I think Wainwright's idiosyncracies (fine word, that!) must be reserved for future comment. "I could go on almost for ever multiplying instances (ía grown-up chum tells me that's the right phrase) to prove the point of this essey, which is streakiness in character I have talked it over with a person who is , generally competent to give one good advice, and (which is better still) doesn't, as a rule, give it oftener than I want it ; and what she says is that I ought to fix my attention on fellows' good strealis,and take as little notice as possible of their bad streakswhich I shan't be likely to imitate if I pay no attention to them. She says one should always be ready to appreciate the good and to I make excuses for the bad—or, if we can't get so far as I excuses, at least not to talk about them. But I'm afraid if I was as good RS all that, I'd die young, like the dis- agreeably virtuous boys in the sort of books given to us by our godfathers and godmothers on our birthdays and if that happened, the person W lio gives me reliable advice would be seriously annoyed by the effect of it. "On the whole, I prefer to be only moderately good, and to give myself a chance of continuing my observa- tions on human nature to a ripe old age."—Frotu a very funny essay entitled "Conceraing other fellows," in the August'• Windsor Magazine," a very sumptuous summer holiday number, which includes complete stories by Jerome K. Jerome, Justus Miles Forman,Robert Barr,ll. C. Bailey, and other favourite novelists, in addition to a large instalment of Rider Haggard's sequel to" She." The articles are many and varied, and a special fine-art feature is made of the pictures of Maude Goodman, of which no fewer than eighteen are finely reproduced. Altogether the number is a splendid holiday com- panion.

div.head: CRICKETERS' LITTLE WAYS.
div.p: CRICKETERS' LITTLE WAYS.

No holiday will be complete without the August "Captain,' w,hich teems with topical articles and stories dear to the heart of boys and " old boys " alike. We follow the serial. "John Baywood," with much interest; the O.H.M.S. story in the present number is a particu- larly thrilling yarn of modern naval warfare. The " Wrykyn " tale', too, is an excellent public school cricket story. The other short stories include a Red Indian yarn, a Woof an extraordinary invention entitled "The Peace Machine." and a humorous anecdote of French militarx maticenvres. "In an Indian Garden" is a pretty-little picture of bird and insect life. "Cricketers' Little Ways" is the title of Mr. P. F. Warner's article, illustrated by "Rip," of " karika- tore" fame. The cycling and photographic editors deal with the subject of holidays and touring, and give much sound advice in both departments. The philatelic editor discourses on "The Stamps of Hungary," and "The Old Fag" has a holiday chat with his readers on the subject of "The 'ldle Month," end makes some suggestions as to the best way to spend it.

Mrs. Chance, wife of Mr. F. W. Chance, the new member for Carlisle, died there on Wednesday. Mrs. Lafone, wife of the Rev. H. P. M. Latrine, vicar of St. St. Cuthbert's, Carlisle, and a daughter of Sir William Broadbent, the physician to the King, also died on Wednesday, after a short illness. At. Leeds Assizes, on Wednesday, Dr. Henry White, of Bradford, was awarded .£1,500 damages against the Bradford Corporation, for injuries sustained in a colli- sion between his carriage and a Corporation tramcar.
