div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
AUGUST sth 1905.

Me. BALFouR did A. BLACK OUTLOOK not think it neces- FOR UNIONISTS. sary at first to specify on Monday the Bills which the Government propose to drop. He enumerated suchmeasures as the Naval Works Bill, the Appropriation Bill, and others of a class that can scarcely be called controversial. But, curiously enough, there was not a word about the Aliens Bill as a measure whith must be passed. Probably Mr. BALFOUR forgot it, or thought it was not worth while to mention a Bill which is not likely to come down from the House of Lords with fresh amendments to be discussed in the Commons. Monday's debate naturally turned on the validity of the proposal to sus- pend the twelve o'clock rule for the rest of the session. Once more, the Opposition pointed out that Mr. BALFOUR has no moral authority for this procedure. His Government exists outside the pale of the Constitution. He is supported by a majority panic-stricken at the prospect of a General Election which cannot be postponed for ever. Most of his colleagues, says the" National Review," "presumably have a shrewd suspicion, though:they bear a brave countenance, that, having finked into places beyond their deserts or capaci- ties owing to circumstances unlikely to recur, they are enjoying their last as well as their first spell of office." "The National Review is a strong and ever violent supporter of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, and this is how it judges Mr. BALFOUR'S policy of evasion." The party placeman and.the party hac refuse to look a year, or even a yard, ahead of them, but anyone who cares to face the facts can see that, if things go on as they are now going on, the Unionist party will sustain such a smashing defeat at the polls as will not only throw it out of office and power for half a generation, but make it a negligible quantity in the State, in which case we should pass under a Radical autocracy." "Dis- trust and disgust in the constituencies," we are told, " are the consequence of the much-vaunted tactics of Mr. BALFOUR, who ii as much in the dark as to the state of public feeling in this

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

country as the CZAR of Russia is ignorant of the sentiments of his subjects." This is much nearer the mark than the assump- tion of "The Daily Telegraph," that the Opposition attacks on the Prime Minister have aroused wide- spread indignation. We find no signs of this indignation except in the columns of the journal. On Monday "The Daily Telegraph" announced with a great air of authority that there will be no , Dissolution this year. Mr. BALFOUR, if he should reach the end of next week without another disaster in the House of Commons, will make up his mind to meet Parliament next February, as though nothing had happened te shake the stability of his Administration. This is not by any means convincing. Mr. BALFours will dissolve in the autumn if anything should happen in foreign affairs which in his opinion will mitigate the extremely bad case he has to present to the constituencies. But it is quite upon the cards that he might come up smiling next Session: with some makeshift of a Redistribution Bill, and go out on that. Oae of the Unionist calculations is that it would be better in any case to resign than to dissolve. It is thought that the Liberals will be placed in a disadvantageous position if they form a Ministry, for then the Dissolution will be their business, and they will have to disclose a programme to the country. Some Unionists cling fondly to the belief that the programme of a Liberal Government will serve the purpose of softening Mr. BALFOUR'S fall, and enable him to recover some of the popular support he has lost. We are quite willing that the General Election should come out in this way, for the issue will remain the same. No manoeuvring on the field of battle will save Mr. BALFourt and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN from overwhelm- ing defeat. The new Liberal Ministry will win a decisive victory for Free Trade. That issue cannot be obscured by the most artful rhetoric against a Liberal programme, for the immediate mission of the Liberal party is to rescue the country from the intrigues which have been directed for the last two years against one of the cardinal principles of its prosperity.

Mr. R. Pierpoint M.P., has been discussing the recent defeat of the Government and, as usual, the French proverb " he that excuses accuses "is veri- fied. After explaining that the hot weather and the absence of members led to a snap division being successful he proceeds to make comparisons which, in the words of Mrs. Malaprop, are " odourous." The nearest parallel to the historic Thursday a fortnight ago that our member could call to mind was Lord Rosebery's defeat on the cordite vote by a majority of seven, which he well remembers. Mr. Pierpoint admits that the Liberal Government of that day might have re- mained in office, but" their position was so weak that they were probably perfectly right in retiring." It is unfortunate that he advances weakness of position as a reason for retiring. Was ever a Govern- ment in a more hopeless state of administrative 1 incapacity and weakness than the one which to- day clings to office by tooth and claw? A few brief years ago it was "the strongest Government of modern times "—numerically—and now it has to shamelessly pervert precedence and use every artifice to keep in office, twill° every bye-election the country through emphasises the utter weani nesa of the nation with its old man of the sea" at Westminster.

Our little note of last week with regard to the positior. of the Corporation as a result of the action with the Ship Canal Company has had the desired effect in that it has elicited an explanation from the Mayor -if several important points which required explaining. It seems that His Worship and the Town Clerk have all along expected that the Corporation would eventually be dismissed from the action. Under these circumstances then it was a bold thing to run up a bill of £6,000, and our warning note was justified. The ultimate verdict with costs against the Ship Canal Company was by no means such a certainty that £6,000 could be safely staked upon it, and even now we are only entitled to hope that the money will be refunded when costs have been taxed. There was a lively discussion on the result of the action at the Council meeting and a considerable opinion that in helping the traders to safeguard their interests on the river a risk had been taken which could only be justified by a successful issue. Putting the question of £ s. d. on one side, how- ever, there is room for congratulation on the fact that the Corporation and traders have secured the verdict. The safeguarding of the river channel is a matter of vast importance to the town and the re-establishment of Justice Byrne's decision is very satisfactory. So long as the river is our main outlet to the sea it remains an asset which must be treasured. Some day we hope Alderman Bennett's dream will come true, and that we shall see Warrington with docks on the Ship Canal and a commerce expanded to dimensions which are at present outside the domain of practical things.

The Water Committee and its contract with Mr Lawson still form a bone of contention. Various Councillors want to know various things, and the Chairman makes lengthy explanatory speeches, but in the end the sum total of information obtained is very small. Only a month ago, Alder man Francoinb said in the Council Chamber that no member of the committee had seen Mr. Lawson's contract or specification of the work. This was a remarkable admission. A sum of £35,000 is alleged to have been paid on a contract the terms of which are unknown to both com- mittee and Council. For two years Councillor Pemberton has been striving with might and main to see this contract and other documents, but he has been denied access through promised facilities for investigation time after time. On Tuesday the contract was produced. Alderman Francomb held up the document and offered it for inspection while the members of the Council gazed at it with an interest and wonder which could hardly have been exceeded had it been the Philosopher's Stone. Alderman Francomb explained that the contract was for £24,000, with a specified rate of payment for extra pumping. It seems that this extra pump- ing has run away with all the money, and worse still the water too has'been allowed to run away. The job at Delph-lane has been throughout mysterious and expensive, and it is a great pity that the Water Committee and the Council have not been made fully acquainted Niel what they were com- mitted to from the commencement of the opera- tions.
'Stockton Heath's threatened boycott of the 10. fare has not materialised, Hence the Chairman of the Tramways Committee's little chuckle 1

* * "Don't play to win; it is not English. Play the game; play for honour. That is English; the game for the game's sake." —Mr. J. L. Paton in " the Manchester Grammar School periodical. * * "Were the Church what by-its profession of Christ's teaching it should be, it would be scourged and mocked, it would be poor and despised ; but it would • be inspired and brave, and beloved of the poor, as Christ Himself was."—" Labour Leader." * 5 * Surely the following is a gross libel on English housewives "To hastily put a piece of meat into a pan a few minutes before the husband comes home, which with a few watery potatoes forms his dinner, seems to be a rooted idea of most women."—" Daily ' Chronicle " correspondent. * * * The Gymnasium Committee was congratulated on its " sweet reasonableness" by Alderman Bennett in an endeavour to pour oil on the troubled waters of physical instruction. Alderman Tinnion was not grateful. He said "the oil poured out by Alderman Bennett was more offensive than ordinary oil." There is still friction, notwithstanding the lubrication. * * * Warrington is leading the way in fine style in the cafe line, however much the town may be behind-hand in other respects. The new King's Cafe in Bridge- street,is a model of comfort and elegance. What with. this, and the Wimnarleigh, the people of Warrington are catered for in a fashion which must make inhabi- tants of other:Lancashire manufacturing towns envious. * * * Bishop Thornton, of Blackburn, is moved to indigna- tion at the sight of the ruined abbeys and monastries which King Henry VIII. destroyed. Speaking at a. Grammar School function on Wednesday his Lorship said that "when he passed King Henry's tomb in Windsor he kicked it '—certainly an original way of expressing his abhorrence of the much-married monarch's depredations. But, added the Bishop, the kick" did no harm to what was beneath."

* * * What several members of the Council referred to as "quick 'itching 'arness " caused considerable dis- cussion at Tuesday's Council meeting. Eventually the recommendation for the purchase of a set was rejected. Councillor Iktaginn pointed out that one of the conditions of hiring is that a pair of horses must. be kept. harnessed and ready to be run down to the Fire Engine Station at a moment's notice. Even a cab-horse might kick against changing from ordinary harness to a " quick 'itching" variety. * * " Works and people are not safe with the flimsy, old-fashioned implements which we have at the pre- sent." This cheerful information was conveyed to the Warrington Town Council by Councillor P. Peacock, who was speaking in favour of the obtaining of tenders for a chemical fire extinguisher. There was, appar- ently, a considerable difference of opinion on the matter between Alderman Smethurst and Councillor Peacock. We shall be wanting an inquiry into the state of the fire-fighting appliances next. * Is Mr. R. Pierpoint, M.P., beginning to entertain doubts about his return to the House of Commons? It would seem so judging by the tone of his remarks at Grappenhall Hayes on Saturday. Referring to the Government defeat he said: "He need hardly tell them that he was present in the House duly represent- ing them—as he hoped he always had done and would do for many years to come." There is always an uncertainty about the future, but Mr. Pierpoint seems to be uneasy about his. From all appearances locally and nationally he has reason to be. Warrington is aching for a change. * * * Our good friend "the Member" is evidently not without egotism. He at any rate is quite convinced that he is worth his place. Perpend "To return- again to the General Election as it affected both him- self and the party he hoped they would do all they could when the time came to return him again. It was not altogether for his own sake—though he had served them well—but in the interests of the party he had the honour of representing and for the good of the country." Well ! Well ! Mr. Keir

ventional. It has always been his'custom to go down to the House of Commons wearing a cap, but on Mon- day he made a more novel departure from the orthodox by appearing in sandals—not strapped to the naked 4 feet after the manner of the Oriental man or the Oeei- r dental child (a la suburbia), but with stockings. The sandals were kept in position by a strap extending ,1 from the centre of the great toe, or top of the sandal, joining with another strap at the ankle. The Socialist i member for Merthyr Tydvil, we are told, declares that the novel wear is very graceful. * * * The borough bowling green is blooming and even the Mayor now looks upon it with a favourable eye- b Once upon a time he said that grass would not grog in Warrington,whicb was a somewhat rash statement. ' Grass will grow as well as orchids and with less atten- tion. However, we are glad His Worship is getting enthusiastic on the subject of bowling greens. has already promised us another, but there is going to ' be a pretty fight over its locality. Every Cotmcillor , wants it in his own ward, of course. Some of them : I will have to be disappointed. There are some parts , lof Warrington where grass or any green thing per- -1 sistently refuses to come forth. 1 Alderman Bennett took an opportunity of allying I himself on Tuesday with the opponents of the Carnegio library scheme. This is the position we have all along thought he ought to occupy in the matter, and we welcome his pronouncement. Councillor Magian takes the other view and wants the library as soon a 9 we can get it. He twitted Alderman Bennett and hie committee with the delay and remarked in his telling way that "if Mr. Carnegie were as slow in granting the money as the committee were in applying for it, the library would be of no use to this generation or 'the next. Personally, we hope the delay will be illimitably prolonged. Warrington is big enough W build its own libraries. 1 During the pulling down of Messrs. Hodgkinson old shop in Bridge-street, in order to expediate mattere work was on one occasion continued throughout the night. During the small horns of the morning the workmen were vainly tying to move a heavy beam t bY means of a rope. Passing tramps were pressed juts service, but even then the beam refused to budge. Shortly afterwards a number of Warrington's pre- servers of the peace were returning home from night duty and having doffed their coats they also lent s hand. The combined efforts of the three parties sufficed to break the rope, and, as Mr. Hallard, wlao tells the story, says, the unique spectacte was seated of our men in blue lying down in company witn tramps.

But it migl4,-" have been at Warrington, and, as I thought of it, cursed the Fates which had sent men to govern TT who could not see a single inch before their noses,alr who sat doddering about the rates whilst, a theft' feet, there flowed neglected a gigantic waterway whi.c-b' might have brought directly to our doors prosperiti undreamed of, and on their threshold lay the meadol which were meant for goldfields and were being bullet,' irretrievably in oozy mountains of promiscuous mud - There is a familiarity about these views and phrage4 which make the identity of " Memnon " easy t° guess!

Personal. The Rev. R. Wilkins Rees contributes anothei most readable article to the current number of the "London Quarterly Review." The subject is the quaint old Cornish poet, parson and mystic, "Hawker of Morwen stow." Mr. Wilmot Lunt, the youngest son of Mr. John Lunt, Latchford, is rapidly winning a leading place in the ranks of our best illustrators. The July "Idler" contains two stories profusely illustrated,and an article on " Whitby " "written and pictured" by him, and he is much in evidence in many a the leading magazines. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC takes away that tired feeling.—(Advt.) _ _

- - Local Artists at the Royal Academy. Among the exhibitors at the Royal Academy this year are Mr. Luke Fildes with his state portrait of the Queen; Henry Woods with "The Venetian Vintage" and two others ; James Charles with "Spring" ; and Oswald Garside with a charming tree and foliage study "Autumn's hollow sigh in the sere wood." Mothers' Meeting Picnic. The members of the St. Peter's Mothers' Meeting had their annual trip to Delamere Forest on Monday. The party started from the school in waggonettes shortly after nine o'clock, arriving at Delamere at about one o'clock. The day being fine, the drive was thoroughly enjoyed by all. Tea was provided, the interval being spent in roaming through the beautiful forest. The outing was greatly enjoyed by all. , ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL

WATERS.—Advt. N.S.P.C.C. Work. The Warrington and District branch of the National society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children has during the quarter ended 30th June, inquired into 86 complaints of neglect, ill-treatment and other wrongs of childhgod, of which all were found to be true, affecting 203 children and 115 offenders. Action was taken as follows :-82 cases were warned, 4 were prosecuted (convicted 4 discharged nil), and none were otherwise dealt tvith. The Society's Inspectors made 566 visits of supervision. Institute of Journalists. The quarterly meeting of the Liverpool district of the Institute of Journalists was held on Saturday at the Liverpool Press Club, Mr. IV. F. Macltray presiding. Reference was made to the loss the district had sus- tained by the deaths of Sir John Willos and Mr. Charles Birchall. Various patters of interest to the profession were discussed. It was resolved to nomin- ate Mr. Xfackray for election as a vice-president of the Institute and a member of the Executive Committee. Delegates were appointed to attead the annual confer- ence at Bournemouth at the end of August,
" PREMIER "CYCLES at 7 guineas startling value.— J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge st., Warrington.— Advt.

Juvenile Rechabites' Prize Distribution. In connection with the Wycliffe Juvenile Tent No. 2214 of the order of Rechabites. An entertainment and prize distribution took place on Monday in the Wycliffe Memorial Hall, when the prizes kindly given by Bros. Wright, Lawton, Riley and Garner, were awarded for introducing new members in the Tent. The Chairman was Bro. William Pearson who gave an address. There were also pianoforte silos, recitations and selections on the gramophone by Mr. Smith. The prizes were presented by Bro. William Wright. A vote of thanks to Mr. Smith, officers and friends was proposed by Bro. Littlewood and seconded by Bro. Low, and carried at the close of a pleasant evening.

UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS.—Advt, • Child's Fatal Fall. Mr. Brighouse, coroner,held an inquest at Warring- ton on Tuesday on the body of Sybil Thorniley, aged 3 years, daughter of William Henry Thorniley, of 9. Greenall street, who died in the Infirmary on Friday midnight from a fractured skull. The evidence of the mother showed that she retired to bed on Thursday afternoon, on account of illness, and took the child with her. When she awoke the girl was missing, and on going downstairs was told that she had fallen out of the window, which had been left open for ventila- tion. The window was an old fashioned sliding one. Mary Douglas, eleven years of age said she was in her back yard about four o'clock on Thursday afternoon, when she saw the deceased leaning out of the bedroom window. She told her to get in, but she took no notice of her. Shortly afterwards she fell to the ground Witness raised an alarm, and the child was taken to the Infirmary. .The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

Ancient Order of Foresters, High Court Meeting. During the coming week the High Court meeting of Foresters will be held at Newcastle-on-Tyne, under the presidency of Bro. W. Sims, High Chief Ranger. It is 27 years since the High Court Meeting was held at Newcastle, on that occasion there were 338 delegates present, representing 531,176 members. During the coming week there will be 800 delegates, representing 923,062 members. There will be submitted for con- sideration Amendments to General Laws, and other important propositions relating to arbitration pro- cedure. Six towns are nominated for the holding of the High Court in 1907 ; 12 delegates are nominated for auditors one of whom is Bro. Councillor Peter Peacock, of this district. Bro. W. Hipkiss, District Chief Ranger, is the delegate appointed to represent this district. He will leave this (Saturday) morning, joining the Chester, Wrexham and Earlestown dele- gates. This Saturday evening the Mayor of Newcastle is giving a reception to all delegates and their wives attending the High Court. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC takes away that tired feeling.—(Advt.)

Warrington Field Club On Saturday the members of the Warrington Field Club visited the banks of the river Bollin at Heatley and Warburton. The Anglers' Association, who have the fishing rights, had kindly given permission for the members to ramble over this section of their preserves. Messrs. Ernson and Greening acted as leaders, and the President, Mr. J. Fairhurst, was also present. Though no new records were made, much that was interesting was seen, and both botanists and entomo- logists had ample opportunity for enriching their collections. The Syrphid family of flies were very well represented. This family includes the hover flies which may be seen balanced in the air with their rapidly whirring wings making a sort of .haze at either side. The close resemblance in colour and markings of many of them to the bees and wasps sometimes causes needless alarm to the uninitiated. Besides three species of Syrphus, Syrittapipiens and Heliophilus pendulus were taken as well as four species of the allied genus Eristalis. These flies, which in the adult state are so bee-like and haunt flowers, pass through their earlier stages as aquatic grubs, the so-called rattail larvae. Moths, beetles, bees and wasps of numerous species were observed. In one spot, on the face of a bank overhanging the river a very fine specimen of a wasp's nest was observed. Despite the extreme fragil- ity of its material it afforded a commodious dwelling to a large number of these busy insects. In another placc a pair of spotted fly.catchers were watched for some time busily engaged in snapping up their insect prey. The most beautiful sight of the afternoon was a large patch of toad-flax in full bloom. The mass, with its long spikes of snap-dragon-like flowers, rich yellow splashed with pale orange, lit with a brilliant July sun, was a thing to live in the memory. Even the most resthetic and scientific have carnal needs, and all were readY for the tea which awaited them at Heatley. Two or three unable longer to keep. away from "beautiful Warrington" returned' by the 7.27 train; the more stalwart brethren tramped through Oughtrington, Lymm, and Grappenhall, reaching Warrington just after nightfall.

div.p: The Examinet, Saturday, August 5, 1905.

Music in the Park. • Crosfield's Brass Band will play the following selections of music on Sunday afternoon, commencing at 3.15 :—March, " Gladiateur," Douglas; chorus, "Be not afraid," Mendelssohn ; selection, " L'Elisir d'Amore," Donizetti ; solo (euphonium), "Sehnsucht," Hartmann; selection, " Memories of Meyerbeer," arranged la) Rimmer ; chorus, "All we like sheep," Handel; hymn, arranged by W. Halliwell ; "God save the King." Conductor, Mr. W. Halliwell. Local Wedding.—Brown —Jago. Considerable interest was centred in the marriage, which was solemnized or Wednesday, of Miss Edith Maud Jago, elder daughter of Dr. Jago, Lamorra, Latchford, and Mr. Edwin Brown, R.8.A., third eon of the late Major Brown of the 6th Dragoon Guards. The wedding took place at Christ Church, Latchford, , the officiating clergyman being the Rev. G. C. Briggs, I assisted by the Revs. Courtney Gale, uncle of the • bride, and Lionel Brown, brother of the bridegroom. ' The service was fulls- chlral. The bride, who was given away by her father, was attired in a dress of , white silk and wore a veil surmounted by a wreath of orange blossom. She carried a beautiful bouquet of , lilies of the valley and white roses. Her ornament was a gold brooch set with pearls, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids, Miss Gale and Miss Jago, wore dresses of pale heliotrope and hats to ! match and carried bouquets of sweet peas. Their I ornaments consisted of gold brooches set with turquoises. The reception was held at Lamorra after which the happy couple left for Barrnouth where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride was attired in a travelling dress of pale grey, trimmed with ruby velvet, and a black hat. Numerous and handsome presents were received, among them being a picture by Mr. Farquharson, R.A., the famous Scotch landscape painter.

LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Adyt. Richmond's Fire Brigade. The first annual outing in connection with the above took place on Saturday, when the party drove to Heatley, via Hon Green and Bucklow Hill. The picnic party, numbering close npon 30, made their headquarters at the Railway Hotel, where there is an exceptionally fine bowling-green. At about four o'clock the party arrived at the hotel, and at ones proceeding with a bowling main, far which several valuable prizes had been arranged. The competition was a very keen one, only two points separating the first and second prize winners,A substantial knife-and-fork tea had been provided for six o'clock by Mr. and Mrs Heaven. Mr. H. P. Hughes presided, supported by Mr. John R. Burnett; the vice-chair being occupied by Mr. John King. Letters of regret at being unable to attend were read from Mr. John A. Ransome, Mr. James William Slack and several othsrs. After tea the prizes were distributed, and the remainder of the evening was passed in a musical entertainment, Mr. W. Pemberton very ably filling the position of accompanist. Mr. R. Warburton. captain of "A. "brigade, proposed, and Mr. 11. Davies, sub- captain of "A "brigade seconded, that a vote of thanks be given to the Picnic Committee (Messrs. W. Wrench, sub-captain, "B "brigade, J. W. Whitney, Mr. Albert Bradley), and to its energetic Secretary, Mr. Clement T. Cox, captain, "B " brigade, for the excellent organisation of the picnic. This was carried unanimously, The prizes were as follows : —lst prize cruet, Albert Bradley; 2nd prize, set of carvers, Walter Wrench ; 3rd prize, set of knives and forks, H. Warburton. 4th prize, pipe and case, William Kirk. Consolation prizes were won by T. Edleston, and Mr. Burnett. Messrs. W. H. Smalley and Albert G. Gartland officiated as referees, and, incidentally, it may be mentioned that much amusement was caused by the extraordinary dimensions of the pegs and ropes used by them. The worthy host, Mr. Tom Heaven, was so interested in these remarkabte pegs that he asked to be allowed to keep them, as curiosities to show to his many friends who come from all parts of Lancashire and Cheshire to the Heatley Green. After a very enjoyable outing the party started for home vizi Warburton Bridge at 10.15 arriving at Warring-. ton, about 11.20. " PREMIER " CYCLES at 9 guineas for Best Grade, unsurpassed.—J. S. GA.RLAND, 51 to 53, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: Druids' -Accldent .Compensation .Award.
div.p: Druids' -Accldent .Compensation .Award.

The monthly meeting of the Druids' Camp Lodge was held on Saturday last at the Higher Angel Hotel, District Grand-Master Bro. Wm. Hankey presiding. D.D.G.M. Bro. John Woods, District Secretary; Bro. E. Allen. District Treasurer; Bro. R. Perdue, District , Trustees; Bros. Wm, Bibby and S. Hankey, Past Dis- trict Grand-Masters ; S. Dunbobbin, P. Langley, J. 1 Wilcock, • E. Pointon, and John Bibby, the Lodge 1 Officers, and a good number of members were present. —At the conclusion of the Lodge business the D.C.S. Rro. E. Allen, said he had been deputed to present to 1 ' Bro. Heesom, who had met with an accident which had resulted in the loss of the left eye, with a cheque for £l5, beinr, the award of the Board of Management from the Accident Compensation Fund of the Order. He regretted that the award was not more, but under- stood that the Accident Compensation Fund had a great many calls, and that fact was against larger sums being granted. This year was the last that the fund would be in operation so far as the Order in general was concerned,but it was optional with the Discricts and Lodges whether they formed one of their own or not.He hoped that the Lodges comprising the District would consider the matter very carefully before they attempted to form one of their own. Ile had no data to work upon as to what this district had paid or received from this Fund that would assist them to form some idea as to the amount each member ought to pay to this fund with the view of having a fund worthy of the name,but hoped that whatever was done would be to the credit of each member of this district. It gave him very great pleasure on behalf of the Board of Management; the District and Lodge Officers to present Bro. Heesom with the cheque. (Applause). District Trustee P.D.G.M. Bro. William Bibby after sympathizing with Bro. Heesom in his sad calamity asked the Lodge to very seriously consider the necessity of keeping up such a fund in the district, so as to be in a position to be able to award certain amounts to brethren who should happen to meet with an accident which might mean loss of employment,and advised them to try if possible to pay a larger amount per quarter so that the district might be able to create such an Accident Compensation Fund that will enable them to ,ruarantee a much larger sum than had been paid the unfortunate brother that night. It might mean a little sacrifice on the part of the members but would it not repay them over and over again to see some unfortunate brother receiving something that would somewhat relieve him? That was the true spirit of Friendly Societies—relieving members in distress. The more they are able to award them the better it would be for the unfortunate ones,and no one knew who might be the next to require it. P.D.G.M. Bro. S. Dunbobbin said he was somewhat disappointed that the Board were unable to grant the brother a larger sum but he supposed that that was as much as the funds at their disposal would allow. The Board's intention with regard to this fund had always been to grant as much as possible; he remembered the time when for a less contribution they granted more than they did now. He supposed there must be more accidents especially in the colliery districts and a larger drain on this fund. He asked them to accept Bro. Bibby's advice and to do all in their power to create a substantial Accident Fund. P.D.G.M.'s S. Hankey, P. Langley and E. Pointon also spoke. Bro. Heesom in reply thanked the board and the District Officers for their kind expressions of sympathy and for the cheque, he could aasure them that this had been a very trying time and the money would in many ways be useful to him. He would never forget this act of the brethren of the Order of Druids. A vote of thanks was accorded the District Officers and visiting brethren for their attendance. Bro. Allen responding dwelt at some length on the position of the district and urged the members pre- sent to do all in their power to uphold the integrity of the Order of Druids in Warrington. The lodge secretary P.D.G.M. Bro. S. Packer gave his statement of accounts which concluded the business of the evening.

div.head: ON SALISBURY PLAIN.
div.p: ON SALISBURY PLAIN.
THE VOLUNTEER ENCAMPMENT.
[BY OUR bPECIAL CORRESPONDENT.]

The members of the Ist Volunter Battalion Prince of Wales' Volunteers (South Lancashire Regiment) left Warrington on Saturday for the annual fortnight's camp training, their destination being Windmill Hill, Salisbury Plain. Tha mounted infantry, cyclist com- panies, cooks, and grooms paraded at the Drill Hall at 9.15 a.m., and, under the direction of Captain Crosfleld, marched to the station in time to catch the 10.25 train. Tue main body of the battalion left in the evening. The men assembled at 6.15 and after an inspection on the lawn in front of the Town Hall they marched through the town headed by the regimental band to the Central Station where they entrained at 7.30. The departure of the men, who were under the command of Colonel Edelsten, was witnessed by a large crowd, who gave them a hearty send-off. The men looked extremely fit and their appearance was favourably commented upon. WINDMILL HILL CAMP. SUNDAY.—Again the Warring- ton Volunteers, officially known as the Ist V.B. (P.W.V.) South Lancashire Regiment, are spending a fortnight under canvas on Salisbury Plain. The departure of the main body was witnessed by a large crowd and the Passage from the park to the Central Station was nearly impassable at times. Prior to starting, the men were medically inspected by Surgeon Major Adams. A splendid run was made by the Midland Railway Com- pany's two trains through the picturesque scenery of Derbyshire. A brief stay was made at Derby where a large number of men left the train. Some amusement was caused by several gallant troopers running like wild animals across the bridge into the street with their water (?) bottles in their hands. Respect for the corps forbids me saying more of this. On starting again most of lithe men crept into the arms of Morpheus and I only opened their eyes at the various stopping places to pop their heads out of the carriage windows and enquire " Where aro we ?" On arrival at Ludgershall, at 4.30 a.m. the few people on the station were startled by the now-familiar " Are we downhearted ? No !" which was raised. The battalion soon formed up and marched off to camp which was reached in about 20 I minutos. After being allotted to their tents, a little refreshment was served out and proved very acceptable. The site of the encampment is about four miles from the Perham Down Camp of last year. The battalion again forms part of the 30th Field Army Brigade together with the Ist V.B. Royal Welsh Fusiliers, the 2nd V.B. Cheshire Regiment and the Ist Herefordshire Volunteers. The battalion is under the command of Lieutenant Colonel J. A. Edelsten, and the other officers are : Majors J. D. Fairclough and B. Fairclough ; Captains F. M. Appleton, G. R. Crosfield, R. Smith, C. F. Cary, H. G. Roberts' P. N. Avery, and A. B. Layton; Lieu- tenants E. E. Ridgway and H. Owen; 2nd Lieutenants R. Lepage, J. T. Picton, and J. Botimphrey ; Adjutant A. F.Bundock, Quartermaster Captain A. F. G. Potter ; Surgeon-Captain J. Adams (medical officer), and the Rev. W. Bracecamp (acting chaplain). There is a complete change in the brigade staff this year, the brigadier being Colonel B. N. North, C. 8., M.V.0., commanding 30th Field Army Brigade; aide- de-camp, Captain and Hon. Major the Earl Fitawilliarn D. 5.0., 4th Battalion Oxfordshire Light Infantry ; galloper, Capt am n P. Gocisal, 4th Oxford Lihht Infantry; brigade-major, Captain E. B. North, Royal Fusiliers; senior medical officer, Brigadier-Surgeon Lieutenant. Colonel P. B. Giles, V.B. ; transport officer and assistant provost marshal, Captain T. Broome Giles, Ist Hereford- shire Rifles; brigade signalling officer, Captain C. E, Bromley, 2nd Cheshire; and brigade cyclist officer, Captain J. B. Bury, Istilloyal Welsh. This morning at 10 o'clock, divine service was held on the parade ground, the Rev. W. Bracecamp (chaplain) officiating. The battalion paraded in a square forma- tion. The preachez spoke for a short time ien " Fight the good fight of faith." He likened the vduty of a soldier to that of a Christian and drew some striking comparisons between the two. In conclusion. Mr. Brace- camp promised to do his best to arrange impromptu concerts, &c., if he was applied to by any of the men The rest of the day was devoted practically to sleeping but a good number left camp for the purpose of visiting the many interesting places in the vicinity. Many of the men had a walk round the other battalions and renewed their acquaintance with their comrades in camp. It is said that the 30th Brigade fraternize better than any brigade that camps on the plain. The battalion has been supplied with sun hats, boots, shirts and braces, and looks very smart in them. Two serviees were held to-day in the Y.M.C.A. tent and were heartily enjoyed by those present. The weather has been splendid, a good breeze modifying the strong heat of the sun. MoNmaY.—The men were early astir this morning and a bright sun welcomed them at 6.45 ‘then the com- pany drill was practised under the company officers. An early devotee of the camera was engaged snapshotting the signallers at practice on the hill at the back of the camp. After breakfast, the battalion paraded in shirt sleeves and, under the direction of the various officers, skirmishing, passing orders, and field signals were practised after a hard match. The signallers, cyclists, mounted infantry and machine gun section were" on their own" to-day and some good practice was done. The men were busy this afternoon preparing for a kit inspection. At night the signallers indulged in a little lamp practice, their new lamps being freely admired by those who watched them. Many men left camp for Ludgershall, Andover, and IBulford, while the Y.M.C.A. again had a crowded " house "at the usual impromptu concert. Cricket, football, &c., were indulged in during the evening. TUESDAY.—To-day we had rather an interesting time. Breakfast was served early and the Battalion was on parade at 8 o'clock. On marching out, the route WAS taken to the south of the camp via Warren Hill to Ash- down Kopje where some interesting manceuvres were gone through. The Mounted Infantry and Cyclists were the "enemy," and, after some brisk fighting,they seemed to be getting the worst of the encounter. On the return to camp, the men were highly complimented by the Colonel who was very pleased with the work. The men show great ability in taking to cover both in advancing and retiring and are very smart in general skirmishing. The signalling section were on the hills at the south of the camp and are greatly improving in their work. Brown faces and rod arms are now quite the order of thoday and the writer does not know what the effect will be at the end of the camping period. A new game has been introduced into camp. The moaftg operandi is as follows :-- rwo ropes of equal length are fastened to a tent peg and a man, blindfolded, is at the end of each. One holds ia his hand a tin box with a marble in it, while the other grasps with fierce deter- mination a bolster. The man with the box rattles it and the other tries to find hi m,and if he succeeds he ig en- titled to belabour him with his weapon. Much amusement is caused by this as our readers may imagine. Rain fell a little during the afternoon, but only enough to damp the grass.

WEDNESDAY.—This morning broke warm and bright and the battalion was early astir. The 6.30 parade con- sisted of a brief battalion drill under Sergeant- Instructors Allardice and Cleaver. The battalion was inspected in full marching order by the Brigadier- General. On the General's arrival, the troops presented arms with fixed bayonets. They were first inspected in line and afterwards formed into quarter column. The General then minutely inspected each company and interrogated several of the men as to various duties. On;their dismissal, the General and his staff went round the different Company lines and inspected the men's kits &c. Later on we had the much talked-of Arnold-Foster medical examination of Volunteers. It has been the main subject of conversation among all ranks since the i beginning of the camp, some being n its favour, but the large majority seem to be against the idea, the pre- vailing opinion being that the Volunteers have enlisted for the defence of their own country, and to ask them to undergo a further special examination to see what percentage of them are fit for foreign service is totally against the spirit of Volunteering. Such a washing of feet among the South Lancashires probably has not been seen for many years. The battalion was ordered to parade with bare feet, loose trousers, and chests bared, so that the doctors could take stock quickly of the physical conditions of each man. It was all taken as a huge joke, and certainly the men looked rather comical as they prepared for the ordeal by a liberal use of soap and water. Colonel Giles, of Here fords, Surgeon-Captain Adam; of the Warringtonituas, and other medical officers examined each man indivi- dually, turning up their eyelids, sounding their hearts making them hop an each leg, and paying special atten- tion to the condition of the teeth, the latter being generally the weakest point among otherwise fit-looking fellows. The report of the medical examination is sumksed to be a private one to the War Office, the result of which will not be known whilst in camp. In the afternoon all the companies were out in the near vicinity of the camp practising semaphore signall- ing. The prize for the neatest company line was won yesterday by "F " Company, this being by far the best.

THURSDA Y.—To-day the rain came and prevented the out-post duty and class and sectional firing which should have taken place. The health of the men remains discipline is well-maintained, REV. W. BRACECAIWP'S ADVENTURE. A peculiar adventure befell the Rev. W. Bracecamp of Warrington, while cycling from camp on Sunday evening. He noticed a Clergyman lying in Ludgershall chnrchiard,and soon ascertained that he had been taken ill during the service, lie found that the first lesson had been read,and putting on the surplice,be continued the service forhis brother clergyman and preached the sermon.

Meeting of the Stockton Heath' Parochial Committee. A meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Com- mittee was held in the Hall Cafe on Thursday evening when there were present Mesgrs. G. Pilling (presiding) J. Whitley, J. W. Bouchier, T. Williams, J. Hallows,F. Pearson, F. Warburton, J. Fairhurst, W. E. Hough (clerk), J. Swinton (surveyor). There was, no business of public interest.

div.head: LAWSON'S CONTRACT.
div.p: LAWSON'S CONTRACT.
ACRIMONIOUS DISCUSSION IN THE COUNCIL CHAMBER.
Councillor Pemberton and the Mayor.

There was an angry scene at the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday between the Mayor and Councillor Pemberton. The minutes of the Water Committee were under discussion, and the Mayor had given an explanation in regard to the much discussed Lawson's contract, when Councillor Pemberton accused him of making statements which were untrue. The Mayor at once demanded a withdrawal, whin) Councillor Pemberton declined to make, and for some time the business was at a standstill, Councillor Pemberton beinr, greeted with cries of "chair" and " withdraw "ashe attempted to explain his position. Subsequently the Mayor declined to listen to the Councillor, saying he was not fit to be listened to and business was resumed. The particular minute which give rise to the discussion read : application was read from the Investigation Committee for production of the following documents. (I) Specification for Mr. James Lawson's contract: (2) orders for 1901: (3) letters written by Water Engineer to Mr. Lawson in 1901; (4) Lawson's Bill for 1901, charging for work done. It was resolved that all the documents with the exception of the specification for Mr. 'James Lawson's contract be produced to the Investigation Committee at their next meeting. Alderman FRANCOMB moved the confirmation of the minutes of the committee, and alluded to the applica- tion from the Investigation Committee for the produc- tion of certain documents. That really was of no account as Mr. Lawson was quite agreeable for the documents to be handed over. (Hear, hear.) The NIAN011: They were all produced at the meeting. Councillor EVANS seconded the passing of the minutes. Councillor MAC: INN asked if it was true that it had been found that it would be necessary to go to arbitra- tion to settle the case between the Corporation and the contractor.
... The MaYon: It has, but it will be a friendly arbitration.

Councillor MA GINN : If there is a contention would it not be far better to be more explicit to the Council ? Up to now we have not been able to get to know what is the amount the contention is about. - _

The MAYOR : Well, I will tell you. All the figures with regard to sinking the four shafts, the concrete lining of the wilts, have been agreed upon between the contractor and the Corporation. The total amount ex- pended over and above the engineer's estimate for the above work is .£1,043 and this is largely due to the bad rock in the alas which was met with in the execution of the works, and which had to be lined. The work of lining adits was delayed as long as possible to see whether or not the rock would weather:

Councillor INIAorgN : Thank you. I have always found you courteous in answering questions, but the answer does not satisfy me. I still have not, and the Council have not got to know the amount in dispute on the whole bill. We were told last night that £ll,OOO had been already paid over the contract. Alderman FitkNCOMB No, no. You are utterly wrong there. Councillor INIAGmr : £24,400 was the contract, £31.000 haslbeen paid. Alderman FRINCOME : -L21,000 is not the amount of the contraot. _ . .

—„ Councillor NIAGINN continuing, said the chairman bad stated plainly a month ago that he did not know the conditions of the contract. He would like some security before the matter went to arbitration or anything else that the members of the Council should get to know what it was they were arbitrating about, and the amount. (Hear, hear.) They might as well not attend these meetings if the committee, officials or anyone else could deal with the matter before the members of the Council knew of it. This was too big a thing to be thrashed out with such secrecy. It might be a friendly arbitration, but the Council were not told the amount of money in dispute and the whole thing was mysterious. The MAYOR said he did not wish to answer for the sins of any committee. They ought not to ask him any of these gnestions. When a man sent in a bill, until it was checked it was not a bill they could say was to be entertained at all. It is refused at present, as it has to be put before the committee as not being correct. Councillor PENtnErrroN: No member of the com- mittee even knows the arncunt ieslisnute. The MAYOR : Have I not just said that it has not been put before the committee because it is not. correct. Councillor PEMBERTON : No member of the com- mittee knows a word about the contract. The whole of it is left entirely to the contractor and Mr. Dens. No one knows on the committee what has been done and what has not been done. They don't know a single word about it. Alderman FRANCOMB : It is not true. Councillor PEMBERTON : Who knows ? What person in this Chamber knows? The MAYOR: Every member of the committee, and you included, know how much we have paid to Lawson. Councillor PENIBERTON : That is all. The MAXOIt : And you saw the accounts at the committee meeting which said that this was the amount certified as being correct. You saw also that there was an account sent in from Lawson month after month which Mr. Deas disputed, and there has never beenany amount paid except ten per cent, less than Mr. Deas estimated we ought to pay. Councillor PENIBERTON : There is one month's bill.
The. Muvoi: There were three of them. Councillor PEmnEtrroN : Yes. Three bills out of three years' work. The nlvon : They have come up month after month.

Councillor PENIBERTON : The bills have not come up every month. I protest against you making state- ments which are not true. (Cries of " Chair," "Chair.") The MAYOR (warmly.)—l will not allow that. You must withdraw that. (Hear, hear.) You were there and saw it. Councillor PEMBERTON : I say.— The MAYOR: You must withdraw it. I mean what I say. Councillor PEMBERTON : And I mean what I say. The MAYOR : You must withdraw that word that I have said what is not true. Withdraw or I will not listen to you at all. Councillor PEMBERTON : Withdraw! The MAYOR : Yes ; you must withdraw the charge that I atu saying what is not true. Alderman TENSION : The remark was, Mr. Mayor, that you had made a statement that was untrue. The MAYOR : You must withdraw it. Councillor PEMBERTON : I am not going to with- draw. (" Chair, chair.) If you will show me— (" Chair.") The MAYOR : I shall not listen to you because you are not lit to be listened to. Councillor PEMRS2TOS :Tf you will point out the time —(cries of" Withdraw,"during which Councillor Pember- I ton resumed his seat). Councillor MAGENN said he did not associate himself with any party on either side. What he said was only his own feeling. The Council should know what the amount in dispute was. The MAYOR: Thera is nothing about this on the minutes. You cannot introduce anything which is not on the minutes. This heckling is not nice for me. 1 Councillor MAGINN : It is not heckling. The MAYOR: Because I choose io give an explana- tion about a matter that is not on the minutes I am to be insulted. I will not have it. Councillor Ma.Grxs : I am not insulting you. I don't like to see these things pass through and you say "They are not on the minutes." Bat it is said now. The MAYOR : Talk to the minutes. I will not allow any more. If you will not be reasonable I will not allow anything which is not on the minutes. The Tow!4 CLERK : Gentlemen, allow me to say that there seems to be a good deal of unnecessary misunder- standing about the contract. It was for £21,400 to begin with ; but other work had to be done. Mr. Lawson has been paid according to his contract and no more. There are no extras. The excess, as the Mayor has said on the adits and the shafts is £1,013. Mr. Lawson has sent to the Corporation not an account buta statement of claim on every possible matter he can think of on the chance of getting money out of the Corporation,and Mr. Dens on behalf of the Corporation makes a similiar claim. it actually makes Lawson appear as a debtor to the Corporation. What information would it be to the Council to give the figures ? They would not be of the slightest use, and I object to the Council discuss- ing figures when I have to take them to arbitration, Councillor MA GINN : And I object to going to arbi- tration without the Council being consulted. The MAYOR : Go on with the minutes. Councillor LORD The Town Clerk has made a state mentto the effect_that there are no extras.

The MANOR : It is not on the minutes. I will not have it discussed. (After a pause.) I will not interfere any more. Councillor Loren: I have heard Lawson say there were a lot of extras. The MAYOR: It is not on the minutes. I will not allow it to be discussed. Councillor LORD : Stick to the truth then. Councillor WILKINSON Mr. Mayor, will you give to the Council your assurance as the Mayor of the Borough, that there was nothing but what can be brought forward fairly and straightforwardly ? The MAYOR: [lava I not said so all along? Councillor PEMBERTON : He has not seen them, SO how can he give his assurance? The MAYori : I don't want to see anything. Alderman lonaNcoml3 : What I object to is the statement that the contract is for £24,000. That was the first part of the contract. The second part is for the pumping of the water. If we have above a certain quantity we have to pay so much a thousand gallons. We happened to get it and consequently we have to nay our just debts. The next item was the hire of plant if it I got to a larger portion still. I object to people saying they are all extras. They are not. They are legitimate ; debts, and it seems such an unfair thing for gentlemen I to be continually saying the contract prioe eras £21,000.

It was never the contract price. The contract price might have been £24,000, £30,000, £40,030, or even £50,000, and I don't think the manufacturers would object if it had been 'P-50,009 if we had got an extra supply of water for it. If we had oaly got one million and aquarter gallons per day we should not have had anything like .C 35,000 to pay, and it is simply because the Water Committee have been successful in getting such a large supply of water that we had to pay a larger amount for pumping. The con- tractor has a perfect right to call for arbitration, and so has the Town Clerk on behalf of the Corporation. If an architect is building a house, and says how much you have to pay, you don't go to the builder and pay him every month what he sends in. I cannot see that there is the slightest wrong in this matter. I don't know that there has been a single penny spent that should not have been spent. I don't care if you do have a special meet- ing to go into the matter of the arbpation. As long as we have a Town Clerk and Water Engineer we are bound to be guided by what they say. We cannot take our law from Councillor Pemberton, although he seems to know more about it than anyone else ; or his opinion about the sinking of wells and edits. We must be guided by professional men. (Hear, hear). Several members rose to speak, but the Mavoß ruled them out of order, and the minutes were spproved. Later in the evening Councillor PEMBERTON moved: "That myself and four members of the Council should have access to all contracts, books, papers, and letter in reference to Lawson's contract, and this cora uittee shall have power to inquire into the vary large amount spent on this contract over and above the contract price of £21,003, and report its (lid inga t.o the Town Council." He remarked at the outset tnat the figure , should be .£21,400. _
Alderootn /.4112A.NC0N113: I object to the resolution. The contract price hss never been £21,400. Councillor PEAmeitrox: Will you priaice the con- tract here? _

Alderman FRANCONIB: Yes. There is n 3 reason why it should not be produced. The NlA.voa r The resolution is notright and cannot be amended now, so it is out of order. Councillor PENIDERTON : Well, in view of the fact that certain other representathes of the ratepayers have also been refused the inspection of the documents and accounts that have been demanded by me The MA.YOR : The matter i. out of order and—

Co-tmoillor PEMBERTON (continuing).— knd in view of the fact that as a result of those refusals steps are being taken by a number of influential ratept^ers to ascertain what is the legal position and rights--(The MAYOR: Well, let them)—of members of the Council and other duly elected representatives of the ratepayers in regard to the matters involved— _

The T I-6;71 do not behave yourself I shall leave the chair, Alderman PRA.NCOMBE : The contract will be pro- dueed or we will continue to have these statements. We have nothing to hide. Councillor PEMBERTON : In view of ttat I will withdraw my motion. Councillor Pemberton was pro- ceeding with some other motions, when the contract was brought in. • Alderman FRANCOMB was proceeding to read from the document when Councillor Lorl protested that it was out of order, another matter being before the Council.

Alderman FRINCONIB : How much longer are yrn two going to act like a pair of lunatics. One says, "read it" and the other says "don't." Are we to be in- sulted like this ? The contract was let for £21,400 for the construction and completion of work," &c., and theu there was a special clause as to pumping, which ran " payment will be made according to the quantity of water pumped." It was the pumping which had cost sum a lot of money, and it was very unfair to say that the contract was for £21,400. That was only for part of the contract. _ .

TOWN : This contract was prep tred on the basis of our being able to obtain 11 million gallons of water per clay, on the advice of Professor Boyd Dawkins. You are all aware that for several days and indeed weeks. Alr. Lawson was pumping four niltiong of gallons a days, so great was the amount of water we found, and it is for that extra pumping that we have to pay. Oonncillor PEMBEIZTON : That boars out rny The AAYOR : I cannot allow any discussion upon this. That is an end of it.

I believe Cross has arranged with his local paper for a.verbatim report of his speech—but if you decide to reprint perhaps you will com- municate with him on the subject.—Yours very truly. J. The year is not named, but the speech referred to is evidently that of the then Presi- dent of the Boon i of Trade (Jr. Chamberlain) on August 12th, 1831. It was duly published by the Club under the title " The French Treaty and ' Reciprocity," with a note that the text had been " revised." _

div.head: SHIP CANAL ACTION.
div.p: SHIP CANAL ACTION.
THE CORPORATION AND THE COSTS OF THE CASE.
Important Statement by the Mayor. M,OOO SPENT.-LIVELY CRITICISM.

At the Council meeting on Tuesday there MIS an interesting argument relative to the action of the Corporation in joining the traders in their tight with the Ship Canal Company. The business came up on the minutes of the Rivers Committee, which contained a report from the Town Clerk, dated July 24th, to the effect that the decision of the house of Lords in the action of Crosfield and Others v. the Manchester Ship Canal Company had been given that morning, and the appeal haebeen allowed, but the Corporation had been struck 9ut of the action.

The AA.YOR proposed the adoption of the minutes and said :—I have no doubt that the Council will ex- pact from me an explanation of the result of the action brought by the Traders and Corporation against the Ship Canal Company, in which judgment was delivered on the 21th July. lam glad of this opportunity of making an explanation, as I believc there is much mis- apprehension with regard to the decision. It should be clearly understood that althoagh the Corporation have been dismissed from the action, an event which was all along anticipated both by me and the Town Clerk, the Corporation have not to pay one penny in the way of costs. The Company have to pay the Traders all their costs in the House of Lords and the Courts below except so far as such costs have been increased by the Corporation being joint plaintiffs. Now the Corporation joined in the action on the advise of an eminent counsel that they had a right of action quite apart from proceedings by arbitra- tion,and their object was merely to compel the company to carry out their obligations tinder the Act. What mean is that the Corporation did not join the action for the purpose of obtaining damages or for the recovery of tolls as the other plaintiffs did. One set of counsel reoresented all the plaintiffs, and the same witnesses - gave evidence on behalf of all the plaintiffs. The Cor- poration did not employ any counsel or call any wit- nesses to prove their case. Therefore it can readily be seen that the costs incurred by mason of tke Corpora- tion being one of the plaintiffs will be very small indeed. The money we have already paid we hope will be refunded. As far as the Corporation is concerned the action is at an end, and there is no cause or matter , which we need take to arbitration. We have won all , round. The Corporation have nothing to claim fo damages, and, as the costs are pooled togeth.r, we hope to come out all right. If the Ship Canal Company carry the action further it will be without the Council. Some editors should be lawyers, as they seem to know everything about these things. Sometimes they are wrong an sometimes otherwise. _

Cotincillor MAGENN: Why on earth did we go into the action at all if we had nothing to arbitrate about? The laf kYOR: We wanted to secure a required depth of the river, and there-establishment of Justice Byrne's decision, and we have succeeded. Councillor MAGINN added that he thought, and a number of those present agreed with him, that it would he as well if in future the Corporation stood outside private enterprise and fought their own case against the Ship Canal Company or anyone else. They had got nothing from the Ship Canal Company bat they had spent money in helping other people who seemed to have got something. They should not run such a risk again. I The MAyori: The Corporation does not need sugges- I Cons of that sort. Wa will not run oar herd into a , noose,
A VOICE: Not again. (Laughter.) Councillor MAGINA : When may we know what the action has cost the Corporation ? The 11Iavon : I am not a prophet. Lawyers have been on this question two years now. _ _
--Councillor MAGENN [IOC; much have we paid already? The TOWN CLERK: About £6,00. Councillor CLEGG : Will we have the money refunded ; . _

, The MAYOR : The whole of it, I hope. Councillor PEMBERTON : It takes a lot of brain power to understand your statements. The MAYOR : The quality of the brain power is secondary if they cannot understand my statements. Councillor PENIIIEBTON commented on the fact that the Mayor and Town Clerk had anticipated according to the statement made, that the Council would be thrown out of this action. Rninent counsel would have to go to the Mayor and Town Clerk for opinion in future. (Laughter.) He protested against the way the Corporation had gone into that action. He would not have objected to the voting of a certain sum of money to support the action of the traders, but he did not think that the Corporation were justified in going into a fight before they knew what, it was going to cost.
The Maxon, said no one knew when going to lam what exactly the cost would ba.. - _

. , COROCiIIOr PEMBERTON said private Orals should fight their own battles. The Council should not have gone to law but voted a certain sum. It had cost £6,000 up to now, but if the traders were going to refund the ' money, it would be a just retarn for the Corporation's I support. Alderman BENNETT said he was of opinion that the Corporation had done the best they could in regard to the matter. It was advantageous to the town as well as several local firms. Fie deplored the fact that the Rivers Committee lacked a sense of due proportion, and cited the case of Manchester as an example of what had been done in the avay of encouraging the trade of the port and dock exteasion. They were so full of the idea of making the river a certain depth that they never looked beyond at tue great Waterway capable of carrying vessels of almost any tonnage. The Committee had taken a small and inadevate view of their daty in this respect—(hear, hear)—and he was afraid that future generations would think they had been very blind indeed to allow the meadows at Arpley to be filled up. Alderman TIN-NION said there seemed to be an impres- sion abroad that the Corporation had rushed into the action with the idea of spending money on behalf or one or two traders. lie pointed.out that there was a meet- ing of the largest traders in Warrington at the Town Hall, and it was their opinion that the Corporation should take up the case, with a view to securing the full advantages of the river. (Hear, hear). Councilloeßertros said there were a number of wchiss on the river now which might not have been in Warring- ton but for the advantages of the river, and he did not agree that the Corporation had no right to take the matter in hand. Alderman SMETHURST said he had been from the first opposed to the Corporation taking any parr in the action. He added that it was due to the excellence of the evidence of the Borough Surveyor that the traders won their case. (Hear, hear.) He hoped they would be magnanimous and with the compensation received build the town a new Warrington bridge. (Hear hoar, and laughter.) In reply to Councillor WILKINSON, the Town Clark said the costs of the action would be taxed in the ordinary way and the money refunded. 1 In replying,the MAYOR said he had hoped that he would have been complimented on the success of the action. There had been considerable anxiety caused to all the committee, and they had all been troubling %hether they were right or wrong. They had won a victory for Warrington so great that none had equalled it for many years. If they had lost all the money they had expended over the matter it would have been money well spent. The river would ( be made sufficiently deep to induce trade and works. A Idivided house soon fell, and he was afraid that all of them were not unanimous with regard to the interests !of Warrington. Every man wanted to run the show in , his own way, some were not altogether honest and straightforward, while others of them talked clap-trap. (Laughter). They were trying to air their little eloquence at the cost of the people and the Corpora- tion. That was not the sort of way to carry on business. Councillor TafaorNe rose to a point of order. He repudiated the suggestion that he had any personal i ends in view. He had only the interests of Warring- ton at heart and he would not allow any man to suggest— The MAYOR: The cap doesn't fit you. Councillor MAGINN : No ; but I feel it. The minutes were then agreed to.

div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A D ktiGEROL;S CHARACTER.

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday P Sculley, described by Superintendent Monaghan as a dangerous character, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, with assaulting Harriet Looker, and also with assaulting railway constables Thomas Rickers and Robert Humphreys. - Harriet Looker, wife of the licensee of the Hop Pole Hotel, Horsemarket-street, said that on Saturday night prisoner called at the Hop Pole. She refused to serve him on account of his con- dition, whereupon he struck her a violent blow on the breast.—Thomas Rickers said that on Saturday night he was on duty at the Central Station at the bottom of the steps. The Volunteers ;core departing. and he had been instructed to prevent people entering the station. Prisoner came up, and upon being refused admittance struck witness. A struggle ensued, during which prisoner kicked him several times. P.C. Humphries appeared on the scene, and prisoner also assaulted him by kicking him.—Prisoner : " He is tell- ing lies. I will put him in the Cemetery and stand the rope."—P.C. Humphries gave corroborative evidence.— Superintendent Monaghan said the prisoner made his 39th appearance. He had spent 13 years in crime, and had had six months time after time for abusing people. He was a loafer, and the publicans in the town were afraid of him.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for six months with hard labour.—On hearing the sentence, Scully exclaimed : "I will get the rope before I have finished with Rickers."
