div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL Motor Cars and Damage to the Roads.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL Motor Cars and Damage to the Roads.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural District Council was held at Bewsev Chambers on Wednesday when there were present Mes.irs. A. Brooks (in the chair), G. Ball, G. Mather, P. Longton,Houghton and Dr. Murray, and Messrs. J. E. Sutton (clerk), F. W. Kerfoot (inspector), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), and H. H. Ramage (assistant surveyor), and Dr. Sephtou (medical officer.) MOTOR CARS AND ROAD-WEAR, A letter was read from the Lunesdale District Council asking for the views of the surveyor upon the question of the damage done to the roads by motor cars. Mr. NEWCOMBE said he bad replied u follows :—T have gone very deeply into the motor car question from all points of view and I am becoming more strongly of the opinion every day that they do not do anything like the real damage attributed to them. There is no doubt that they do raise the chippings and bind- ing in dry weather but in ordinary weather they do absolutely no damage and cause no wear. I would suggest this : Is not a car (probably owned by some- one paying big rates and big income tax) entitled to an amount of wear equal to an iron tyred vehicle? I think so. I think that taking the year round they do less damage than an average omnibus or conveyance carrying the same num- ber of passengers. It is a well-known fact that when macadam roads are soft in winter the biggest part of the wear is not on the top but in the bed of the road, so that nearly all the damage done by iron-tyred vehicles does not show. It would be understood that motor cars do none of this. Supposing anew road twelve inches thick be constructed of entirely new metal, all angular and not less than two inches in size. If ten years afterwards this same road be cut across the stone would be found (in a heavy traffic road) to be worn into round marbles most af the way through, and if not sheeted in the meantime will probably have thinned down to G incheq. Of course it wilt be seen that rubber- tyre(' wheels would not affect the stone at the bottom of the road. The fact of the stones being round below the surface proves that the wear is caused by shock and vibration. In years gone by we kept several men doing nothing in the summer but picking loose stones and binding. During the last two years al) have had none No doubt heavily-laden iron-tyred motor lurries do an- immense amount of damage, and I often see in our dis- trict deep groves for miles in the macadam caused by these vehicles, and in soft .veather it may be done by one vehicle. I think rubber tyres do no damage beyond that which we see on the surface. THE RECENT DROWNING FATALITY AT WOOLSTON. The CLERK read a letter from Mr. S. Brighouse,county coroner, stating that on the 15th July he held an inquest at Woolston upon the body of a man who was drowned in the river. The jury added to their verdict that in their opinion the footpath along the side of the river is dangerous. . Mr. KERFOOT said the footpath was broken in places through cattle trampling over it. It was decided to refer the matter to the deputy Lieutenant of the county. DEFAULTING PARISHES TO BF. SUMMONED. The CLERK reported that Rizton and Croft had not met the calls served upon them. He always had a deal of trouble from those two parishes, who when other parishes had paid four calls had not met a single one. It was decided to summon both parishes. HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. Dr. SEPHTON reported that during the month there had been 26 births and 29 deaths. The death rate was equal to 31.3 per 1,000 as against 32 the average of the past three months and 37.9 for the corresponding period of last year. Nineteen deaths occurred at the county asylum, Winwick, exclusive of which the death rate was equal to 10.3 per 1,000. Tha Inspector reported that he had taken three samples of water from Phipps Brook,Burtonwood, and forwarded some to Mr. Carter Bell for analysis and he reported as follows. Taken below the brewery : This is a very had sample of sewage having a very bad odour of sulpharated hydrogen. Taken above the brewery: This a very bad water contaminated with organic matter. Taken ouposite Rodlev's Farm : This is a very bad sample of sewage having A very strong odour of sulphur- ated hydroeen. The Medical Officer was instructed to confer with ! the Surveyor with a view to the preparation of a ' scheme for the extension of the Burtonwood Sewers. I

div.head: KING'S CAFE. INAUGURAL DINNER.
div.p: THE KING'S CAFE. INAUGURAL DINNER.

The re-building of Messrs. Hodgkinson's shop in Bridge-street has afforded the Warrington Cafes Limited an opportunity of opening a new cafe, which they have named the King's Cafe. This has been established in the basement of the new and commodious shop and in making a really attractive dining hall the architects and decorators were faced with great difficulties. That they have ably surmounted the obstacles which presented themselves will be readily granted by all who visit the premises, and Warrington has reason to be proud of the latest adition to its cafes. The room will provide accommodation for 200 diners. The in- augural dinner was held on Saturday evening when the architects, decorators, workmen, &c.. were entertained by the directors of the Cape Company,Mr.J.W.Hayward presiding over a large gathering. An excellent repast was provided after which the evening was pleasantly spent in speechmaking and song. T'ae usual loyal toasts were honoured on the proposi- tion of ale CHAIRMAN. " WARRINGTON CAFES." This toast was entrusted to Mr. HODGKINSON who in submitting it said he felt that the opening of the King's Cafe marked a red-letter day in Warrington—(hear,hear) —though to many it might appear an important occasion He thought the enterprise and pluck of the Warrington Cafe's Limited, particularly of Mr. Hayward, deserved the greatest credit. He thought that the company were doing a good work, and one which would have a wide influence and far reaching results. Warrington was a town which had few attractions when set side by side with the towns such as Manchester and Liverpool and he believed the enterprise of the War- rington Cafe Co., would be a commercial and social success. (Applause.) He felt that the new premises would be of the greatest service to the business com- munity of the town, and that it was bound to have beneficial results, and he thought that if other persons in the town would only show the same enterprise the town would be better for it. (Applause). The toast was heartily drunk. Councillor BROUGH, on behalf of the chairman and directors of the company, returned thanks. The success which had attended the opening of the Winmarleigh Cafe had shown the great need which existed in the town for such buildings. Ho thought the new cafe reflected the greatest possible credit upon the architect, decorators and workmen. (Applause). "THE BUILDERS AND DECORATORS." Captain SAVAGE proposed "The builders, decorators, and architects," and in doing so paid a high tribute to the excellence of the work in each department. In responding Mr. HESKETII said he felt that the whole of the arrangements connected with the Cafe, from an architectural and decorative point of view; were of the highest order. He congratulated Mr. Hodgkinson upon the palatial premises which he had had erected. He regarded the new building as one of the noblest in the town, and the Cafe as second to none in the north of England. (Applause.) Mr. GARRETT replied on behalf of the architects, and wished the cafe and Mr. Hodgkinson every success. Mr. BALLARD and MT. MAILE replied on behalf of the workmen, the former recounting some humorous incidents which occurred during the erection of the building. "TOWN AND TRADE OF WARRINGTON." In proposing this toast Mr. BIRTLES said he was proud to see Warrington progressing. (Hear, hear.) He thought the victory gained by the traders of the town in action against the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany, would have a far reaching and beneficial effect upon the town—(hear, hear)—as the traders would be able to use the river as it ought to be used. He remembered ship-building yards in Warrington and with the deepening of the channel of the river he hoped to see ships again being built on the banks of the Mersey at Warrington. Educationally Warrington was taking the lead. In the past the Warrington Academy had sent men forth into the world who bad set a noble example. In the school of art we had sent out men who were second to none, and he thought the town had an excel- lent prospect before it. He thought if the Corporation I would only pass plans of some architectural merit the town would become beautiful in spite of itself. Ile hoped the town would continue to prosper and progress and that it would become a town of first importance in the country. (Applause). " THE LADIES." Mr. C. ROYLANCE proposed the health of the ladies, coupling with the toast the names of Mrs. Hayward and the Misses Hayward. The toast was heartily drunk. Mr. W. ROBERTS, in responding, said he thought the success of the cafes had been in a large mew. Ire due to the ladies who assisted in the management of them. They sometimes heard its said that ladies were good as wives, but they re re not to be trusted with business. He ventured most emphatically to contradict that assertion. (Hear, hear.) Be was proud to testify that the Cafe Company had an admirable staff of ladies from the highest to the low( st whose hearts were in the work. They were that night entering upon a new phase and he believed the new undertaking would prove not only a flnanciadsticcess but of social benefit to the town. He posed as a temperance reformer and believed that by giving his best endeavours to promote the success of the Warrington Cafes Ltd,be was doing more to promote the real, true and best interests of temperance than by speaking at temperance gatherings. (Applause). During the evening songs, &c., were given by Mr. C. G.Gemson,M r.P. George, Miss E.lll iller, Miss L. Plinston, and Mr. Willett and violin solos by Mr. T. Boothroyd. Mr. Wilkes acted as accompanist. At the Warrington Police Court on Monday the Magistrates granted an application for a music licence for the King's Cafe, it being the intention of the directors to organize nightly concerts for the entertain- ment of their customers.

DESCRIPTION OF THE PREMISES. A description of the commodious new cafe will pro- bably afford interesting reading to our readers. The main dining apartment is formed in buys the ceiling beams forming bold panels. At the ends of the beams a handsome corbel or truss has been fixed to support the same, and at intervictions bold pillars have been fixed and framed in rich pannelled work with fine caps to support the beams. A portion of the room has been partitioned off so as to form a fine smoke room. The fitments, all in white wood, comprise panelled dadoes, and magnificent counters and cabinets for the display of the various goods usual in such establishments. Another feature is a recess with elaborate coffee counter and cabinet. This abuts upon the kitchen offices, which are furnished with everything up-*O-dats required for carry- ing on the business. There are also ladies' cloak rooms and lavatories all fitted up in the latest and most sanitary manner. The cafe proper is well-lighted by the new Luxen prismatic lights which enable a visitor to see clearly to all parts of the premises. The venti- lation has also had special attention and secures perfect airiness and comfort. . . .

The decorations are of a very elaborate character, no expense having been spared to make everything please the eye; restfulness throughout has been the point aimed at and it has been achieved. The ceiling panels are tilled in with raised material framed with a mould- ing forming a broad stile round each, the return of each beam being filled in with bold egg-and-tooth raised material. The whole has been painted a beauti- ful soft light grape tone, full of bloom, but perfectly dead, except the centre of the panels, which is enamelled to show the raised materials to better advantage. The fiats of the beams and returns to enrichments are in solid deep gold, toned down to copper, whilst the corbels, caps of pillars and pillars are enamelled to the same grape colour, together with all other fittings and enriched with gold and silver. Some of the enamelled work is perfectly dead and this treatment gives a peculiar richness to the whole. Another unique and striking feature in one of the long walls over the cubicles is a very bold frieze formed in panels of heavy raised materials representing ancient tournament scenes, which are treated in heraldic colours, gold and silver. Other panels of the same material repre- senting vintage are treated in old ivory colour 5041 gold. The light grape-coloured woodwork beneath, surrounded by fumed oak cubicle fitments upholstered in rich, light blue tapestry, gives an air of luxurious- ness to the whole. The floor is of polished pine blocks. Messrs. Hesketh and Son, Limited, are responsible for the whole of the decorations and are to be congratu- lated upon the result of their labours. Messrs. Wright, Garnett and Wright were the architects for Messrs. Hodgkinson. Limited, for all the internal fittings, and Messrs. Fletcher,Riissell and Co. supplied the fittings in the kitchen. Mr. T. Birtles, of Sankev-street, has re- produced some very pretty George Sheffield sepias into the panels along the wall facing the entrance aoor.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

• Anniversary Services. On Sunday, the Rev. C. L. Stowe, of Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church, celebrated the completion of the first twelve months of his ministry in Warring- ton and special services were held, the pastor occupying the pulpit on each occasion. In the afternoon a musical service was held. After a discoinso in the evening on the story of the prodigal son the rev. gentleman gave his audience a brief outline of the circuit's w(,rk during the past year. The collections for the day amounted to £3 15s.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was a fair attendance at this meeting on Sun- day, when Mr. G. Smiley presided and addressed young men especially upon the importance of abstaining from the use of iotoxicating drinks. Mr. J. R. Wolstencroft. Swinton, spoke upon "The religion of daily life." A religion for one day in the week was a very poor one and coeld not be of Christ. "What would Jesus have me do ?"—"that which was right and just." Jesus was obedient to His father, faithful to His love, lived, worked, suffered and endured; so must we, in our daily life. These examples were before us, and if we tried to follow them, our lives would be happy and we should prove a blessing to our .fellows, and God would be honoured. Mr. W. Miles. the Rev. J. Yonge, and the secretary also took part in the meeting. In the absence of Mr. Payton, Master W. Pearce presided at the organ

"This in future
"The truth, monseigneur." "Gone where ?"

"iiel;-c;m-e-f-o; her, monscigneur." "Look you! You are mad! I came-----" And then he stopped short, a sudden thought having struck him. "Treachery," he groaned, and he leant back against a chair. "That letter! It was from Marie. Mad woman that she is!"

Jocelyne gazed at him earnestly. "My mistress is in some cruel danger,you think, monseigneur ? " she said, pleadingly. "You will save her?" "Yes," was the stern answer. "Yes, I will save her," and ere the other could sax another word, the heir to the throne had turned and vanished in the night. "It is her doing," he muttered, "but I will have justice done here and that right soon." A few steps further up the street his carriage was waiting, and he sprang in. "To the Palace," he said, sharply. The door was closed and the vehicle rolled

away. "Whore have they put -ler ?" he said to him- self. "It is Marie's doing—of that I am sure. Poor fool! What does she expect to gain by that step? Bah! She dare do nothing—she dare do nothing," he mused, and the same conviction was with him as the brougham stopped and as he stepped quickly out and entered the palace, rousing up his valet, who, not expecting his master's return, looked upon him for the moment as if he were a visitant from another world, trembling like a suddenly jerked blanc-mange. The Prince turned upon the eervitor sharply. "What is wrong, Jasmin ? What have you been running from ? "

"Monseigne'ur, I--" "There, it is all right, Ja,smin," exclaimed the Prince, and he passed on into a brilliantly - lighted salon, when his attention was taken up by a sound without. "Who is there ?" he said, quickly. The valet disappeared, but speedily returned. "It is Captain Molyneux, your Royal High- ness," he said. "Let him come in," said the Prince, and the Captain, in the travelling uniform of the Royal Guards, entered the apartment as the Prince dropped on to a couch. "you come?" he began. "From Reineville, your Royal Highness." "And the King is well ? " The officer bowed. "His Majesty charged vie to give you this letter, Sir." The Prince took the missive, sealed with the Royal Arms. c'Molyneux," he said, as he opened it, "who is Captain for the night?" "Delavoye, sir." "Hah ! Our good friend Delavoye, whose sister —but absurd, no matter. Do they not say that he is like me ?" The officer bowed, but apparently his sign of acquiescence was lest on his master, who was eagerly scanning the letter he had just received, and as he grasped the contents, his features relaxed, and he gave vent to a cry of joy, for the communication ran:

"My dear Son,—l write this to you as your father as well as your King. Long have I thought over this matter of your marriage with Madame Yolanda. My son, everyone should be happy in this world, and I regret that I have so long withheld happiness from you by my refusal to consent, but though my permission has been delayed, you have it now."

The Prince glanced up from the writing. "Afolyneux, he exclaimed, "you will come with me." "Yes, your Royal Highness," and as the Prince strode out of the room, the Captain followed to the courtyard where the escort was waiting, thence to the guard-room door. For a moment the lieutenant in charge did not recognise the Prince, for the uniform he wore was the same as that of the Captain. "You said that it was Delavoye," said the ! Prince. "Yes, your Royal Highness." "Good," and the Prince thrust open the door almost savagely, to see the Captain of the night ' motionless in a chair without his coat—drunk ! or drugged. Molyneux could do nothing to save his brother officer, because the Prince was before him, and au i he said was:
"111, your Highness." The Prince gave a contemptuous shrug of the shoulders.
-..—_,.... "Ill," and he touched the unconscious man on the arm. "No, Captain Delo.voye id' not ill, but drunk. Place him under arrest."

Molyneux turned to the door- with machine like obedience and called for the Sergeant of the Guard, who hurried up. "Sergeant," began Molyneux, but the Prince waved him aside, and began to (paestion the non. commissioned officer. _ _

"When did you come on duty?" "At six, monseigneur." "The Captain supped here?" "Yes, monseigneur." "Alone ?" "No, monseigenur." "Then with whom?" "With a lady, monseigneur.' "You knew her ?" The Sergeant bowed. "It was the Princess Marie, his sister, monseigneur." "That will do," and as he spoke the Prince turned to leave. "Come, Molyneux," he said. "That explains it all." The Captain looked a multitude of inquiries, but unfortunately for his curiosity it is not given to officers, even of the Royal Guards, to press interrogations when Royal personages are con- cerned, and consequently he did not ask what was "all" and what it explained. But early on the following morning, had he possessed the ear of the magician, he might have learnt the truth.

- As it happened, Alexander, despite his intense disquietude, was persuaded that he could do nothing that night, and that only the morrow would solve the enigma, and his surmise proved correct, for there was an early caller at the Palace in the person of Princess Marie. "I have come," she said, "because of our old friendship---" He stopped her there. "I wish to hear nothing of that," he said. "You came to this country with a ready-formed ambition as regards myself—if ambition it can he called—and which only you entertained."

"But," she exclaimed, "you mistake my inten- tion in coining here. I wish only to plead fa= my brother who, I learn, is in disgrace.' The Prince watched her keenly. "You supped with him last night?" "Yes." "He was found drunk—on duty." "But you will pardon him?' she said, tremulously. "The penalty might be—death. We live in disturbed times, only--" "Yes?" she exclaimed,

"Only Delavoye is not to blame." She waited for him to continue with parched lips, but he seemed in no hurry to go on. "Sit down," he said, calmly. "I have much to say to you." And she obeyed, mechanically sinking on to a couch and watching him keenly the while as he crossed to the wide window and looked out on the stretch of park-like country which flanked the city on the west. Suddenly he turned to her: "Where is. Yolande " he demanded, fier,,elv. "Yolande ! Ido not know." "You lie!" he exclaimed, savagely. "Tell the truth or else—your brother shall die." "But he is not to blame !" she cried. "No, for you drugged him last night, in order that you might secure his cloak, so that you could disguise yourself and act an ignoble part: but, clever though you arc, you will thwarted here," and he advanced to her and seize her wrist. "Listen! A word from me, and Dela- voye will be shot—to-morrow morning—and I will give that word unless you tell me all." "Alexander!" she cried. "It was for your sake, and----" "The truth," he said, sternly. "Where is Yolande ?" She hesitated a moment longer. "Where is she ?" he repeated. "At the Convent of St. John."

Half-an-hour later the porter of that excluded retreat was aroused to admit the Prince and his aide-di-camp, and the Superior, obeying the visitor's instructions to let him see Wand°, was constrained to lose the beautiful stranger whorn she le d been assured would remain there for all time. As they drove away together the Prince turned to his promised bride: "I feared that you were lost to me," he said. "And I--" she began, and stopped, for she could say no more; but she was smiling through her tears.
:ETRE END.]

Mr DEAL CHM You will remember that a week or two ago I wrote you a special letter, regarding the beautiful watch and books that I shall give to the children sending in the largest number of names of new members before August 31st. Well, I have received a very good list from Thomas Thacker. This is capital, and I have sent him some more forms to fill in with further members, if possible. I think, Thomas, that you stand a very good chance of a prize, unless some of my nephews and nieces work very hard for the remaining weeks. I have received a very nice letter from Violet Jorderson, telling me all about her fiets. She has had a canary, jackdaw, and a goldfinch, at variohi times. I had a jackdaw once, and he tried to swallow my watch, but, of course, this was quite impossible, so he made up his mind to taste a part of it; he, therefore, broke the glass, and tried to swallow some, but the glass stuck in his throat, so that I had to have him killed, as he was suffering so much. I have also had a letter from Ivy Nichols. You are very welcome, Ivy, but you call yourself a "little one"; now, by your writing, I should say you were sixteen. lam very glad that you are going to have such nifte holidays in the country. I was pleased also to receive a letter from Doris Nichols, who invites me to go and see her when in the country. This I should be very pleased to do, but she has given me no address. T have also received correct solutions to puzzles from several of my little friends. The solutions to puzzles and "Rather Contra- dictory" will appear next week, when prizes will be awarded. I will give a prize to the boy who sends in the best pen and ink sketch of a dog, and a prize to the girl whcs makes the prettiest toilet-box out of a cigar-box; these to be sent in by August 15th. 1 With love; from UNCLE NED.

It was too early for anyone to be Rtirri ng in the little place, but Clytie's manner was that of one who was not to be deterred, even if there had been somebody to see her. She was very, very much in earnest. She stepped up to the little shop and felt about its door and window with her trunk for a moment or two. Then she drew back from the door with her head held low, and lunged forward with a tremendous rush. The door was not elephant-proof, and so it crashed in- ward without trying to keep up even the appearance of resistance. Clytie followed without any haste, but w,th every evidence of complete satisfaction. She had found her way into an elephant's paradise, and she knew it. In another moment she had overturned the boxes and jars which stood on the counter, and was stuffing the sweetmeats into her greedy mouth. She had broken into a candy and fruit store. She seemed to realise that it only happens once in ifilifetime of an elephant to have the freedom of a confectioner's shop, and she acted as if she intended to improve the opportunity to the utmost. She sampled everything she could reach—and she could reach almost everything in the shop—and she did not think of stopping merely because the man who owned the candy rushed hurriedly into the store from the back room, and then rushed still more hurriedly out again, yelling, "Ow! Ow! at the top of his lungs. Nor did she stop when the whole neighbour- hood took up the worthy man's cry of "Ow! Ow!' She went on eating and eating, until a little man, named Job, came running up, and cried out in a sharp voice; ..

Hi, there, Clytie. What d'ye mean? Come out o' that, now, cl'ye hear?" Then she backed out in a great hurry, and looked very rauch afraid of the little man, for he was her keeper, and she had great respect for him, and knew he could punish her if he chose to do so. But, after all, sne had eaten her fill of candy, and so, what did it matter. But the question was, how did she manage to distingr4sh a candy-store from any other? Of course, she could not read .the sign over the window, and it was almost unlikely that she could tell by the smell, even when she reached the spot. The difficulty is, how' should she have known the way to go directly to that store? Everybody was puzzled for a long time, but at last the man wno kept the store offered the solution. He had fed an elephant from his shop as many as twelve years before. Was Clytie that elephant? More inquiries were made, and the fact discovdred that she was

div.p: the elephant that had been fed there twelve years earlier. Her memory was better than her gratitude. • —4-- THE FIRST ROSE OF SUMMER. "Oh, dear! is summer over?" I heard a rosebud moan, When first her eyes she opened, And found she was alone. " Oh, why did summer leave me, Little me, belated? Where are the other roses? I think they might have waited!" Soon the little rosebud Saw to her ,surprise Other • roses opening, So she dried her eyesi Then I heard her laughing Gaily in the sun, "I thought the summer over; Why, it's only just begun!"

HOW POLLY & PETER KEEP HOUSE" My uncle is threshing with Freddy; My mother has gone to the fair; I've vowed to be steady as steady, And baby, she's tied in her chair. I must brush up the hearth to look neater, And put all the tea-cups away— There's no bne to help me but Peter, And Peter—why, Peter's at play. Just hear how the turkeys are crying, And the calf is as hungry as two! I'll see if the cherries are drying, And then there's the churning to do. In summer we churn in the cellar, So baby can come there to stay— I must think of a story to tell her While Peter—but Peter's at play.

It is time that the chicken was over, And my mending is scarcely begun— Here's Peter come up from the clover, And we never have dinner till one! Evidence of the esteem in which the late Mr. David Davies, whose death we recorded last week, is held, was afforded on Saturday by the large attendance at the funeral which took olace at the Cemetery. Leaving the Infirmary at 2.3o;the cortege proceeded to the Cemetery, general regret being manifested on every hand. The principal mourners were :—Messrs. Alfred Davies (Halifax). Jack Davies (Walkden), Wm. Davies and J. W. Davies (brothers), and Messrs. T. Davies, J. Davies and Charles Isherwood (nephews). Messrs. Newton, White, and Lingard represented Messrs. div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
A VINDICTIVE TRAMP AT ST. HELENS.

When given in charge three months ago for being on Mr. M'Kinnell's farm premises at St. Helens under suspicious circumstances a trainp named Wood said, " When I come out, if I get seven years, I'll set fire to your—place." Wood was sentenced to three months' imprisonment, and was released from gaol on Tuesday morning. On Tuesday night Mr. M'Kinnell saw a man secrete himself in a stack of straw. He informed a police constable, and the man, who was arrested, proved to be Wood. There was found upon him a box of matches, but no pipe or tobacco, and Chief Constable Ellerington pointed oat to the St. Helens magistrates on Wednesday that the circumstances would Is vi one to supoose that j Wood had intended to carry out his threat. There was a bad record against the prisoner, who was remanded for a week.

div.head: GUESS.
div.p: A GUESS.
Extensions Advocated.
The Examiner, Saturday, August 5, 1905.
LAM. RIGHTS RESERVED. j THE ETIQUETTE OF COURTSHIP &
MARRIAGE IN AMERICA,
MRS. C. N. WILLIAMSON. (Author of" The Barn Stormers," " The Lightning Conductor," te.).

If an English girl, who had not yet made her bow to society, should be taken to New York or some other large American town, there to blos- som out as a debutante, fall in love, and become engaged to an American, she wou:d be sur- prised at some of the new customs she must comply with. Let us suppose the case of a young girl of good birth, whose parents have moved in the best society of their own country. When she is seventeen her parents move to America and take up their residence in New York. By the time the family has established itself in the new home, and collected a large circle of acquain- tances, it is time for the young girl, now eighteen, to make her • debut. _ _ _

.„ Already her mother—a clever woman fond of taking up new fads—has amused herself by adopting many American customs. Among others, the has engaged for her pretty daughter. a trained nurse instead of a maid. This grand person will look after the young girl's health during the fatiguing gaieties of the first season, ,yet will not be above dressing her hair, and performing all the other duties of a lady's maid. She will arrange the debutante's bath, with strengthening essences in the water, the tem- perature of which will be tested with a thermoL meter. She will have a cup of steaming broth or chocolate ready for the important young per- son on the return from a ball ; she will banish sleeplessness with mirage ; she will know all about " symptoms." and be able to say when rest is absolutely necessary.

....... pi n!. One ies eacn watch of brilliants, but it still remains for the i bridegroom to present them with their bouquets and the little muffs which go with their cos- tume, the idea bell= that everythinz earrisci by the bridesmaids must come from him. He also gives his best man a handsome souvenir, and chooses some less costly remembrance of the occasion for each of the six ushers. A 'WEDDING REHEARSAL. A few days before the wedding, the girl bids her bridesmaids and her Matron of Honour to lunch. Never, surely, was there more happy laughter. They all remind each other of funny incidents in their girlish experience together they drink the bride's health if it is but in lemonade ; they discuss with eile•''er interest not only the details of the wedding, but the dinner which the bridegroom is to give that same night to his ushers and best man. • It is the evening which follows these festivi- ties " that has been set aside for an important event. All the wedding party assemble at the bride's house, and go thence to the church for a thorough rehearsal of the wedding. Only the clergymen are absent. All is carefully prac- tised, and each detail gone over several times, that there may be no hitch when the real hour arriyes. The bride's train has been measured, and some drapery of exactly the same length is tied to her waist and left to trail. • Alter this experiment there is no danger that her dress may be stepped upon. Meanwhile, during the last few weeks pre- sents have been falling thick as hail, and be- fore , the wedding they are shown to a few friends ; also they are to be formally "on view " upon the day itself, with plenty of de- tectives ,in plain clothes hovering in the back- ground. An hour before the marriage ceremony the six ushers arrive at the church, looking very smart, with their wedding favours. They show the ladies to their seats, and when each pew is full to overcrowding, they move swiftly •up the aisles, running white ribbon through the ends of the pews, until the waiting throng is fenced in with a satin lattice. For days they have practised tying bow knots, and succeed in making effective butterfly bows at the chancel end of the long line of pews. THE FINALE. They have only just finished when the music of the wedding march begins. The bridesmaids appear, and after them walks the young Matron of Honour, proud of her responsible office. Then comes the bride, with her father. The bridegroom meets her quickly, and the " be- trothal " part of the marriage service (amended it little to suit Americans) begins at the bottom .of the chancel sten. It is not till later that the bridal party move up nearer to the altar. It is over at last, and there is a rush to the big house " on " Filth Avenue for the recep- tion. The elaborate church decorations were all white, but the flowers at the house are gay with colour. The guests linger, but in two hours evetyone save the intimates are gone. The bride and groom have told none of the out- siders what they intend to do, but what they really do is to stay and dine quietly with the family and the bridesmaids and the ushers, all of whom have been invited to remain. Soon after dimmer, however, the newly married pair take their leave, under as plentiful a shower of rice and slippers as if it were England and not America. With the vanishing of bride and bridegroom, one might think that the evening was ended, but not so. The bridesmaids and ushers stop for a dance, and who knows how many more en- gagements will not have been made before mid- night?

div.head: AN AMERICAN "AT ROME."
div.p: AN AMERICAN "AT ROME."

The girl's debut in society is acccmplished by nothing more thrilling than au" afternoon At Home given in her honour. But such an At Home ! Nothing like it wits ever seen- in Eng- land. She begins to realise that something rather remarkable is to be expected, when her floral offerings pour in, on the mottling of the eventful day. Before the hour at which the guests arc invited to welcome her into society, she has re- ceived no less than two hundred magnificent bouquets. Many are composed of roses— American Beauties," with thick green stems long enough to be used as walking-sticks, and tied together with heavy satin ribbon, eight inches wide. A wonderful paling of tall roseti and lilies—all sent in to the girl with good wishes or witty verses—lines the.entire wall of the big drawing-room when the guests begin to arrive, and there are tables banked with vio- lets, gardenias, and all the flowers most fashion- able to offer debutantes.

Fifth Avenue is packed with the carriages of her friends. Many more young men attend .the At Home, than would deign to appear in Lon- don. There is dancing, and the affair is a huge iiiccess. Next morning there are paragraphs bout it in the papers, several of which have contrived to secure the debutante's photograph. She is called a " Rosebud," and when she is inclined to resent this as a liberty she is told that all débutantes are technically " Rose- buds ;" that she will now be asked to " Rose- bud " dances, " Rosebud" dinners, and Rosebud "theatre parties.
A DELIGHTFUL NOVICIATE.

Soon she finds herself in a whirl of gaiety. She has more invitations than it would be pos- sible to accept, unless she had that great con- venience to a girl in society, an astral body. To her surprise, half of these invitations do not include her mother. A girl issues an invitation to a dinner in her own name, and there is but one chaperone present, some popular young married woman, perhaps a bride of a few months. By and bye the new Roesbud gives such dinners and dances herself, for her mother wishes to fall in with all the reigning customs. As a Rosebud she is taken seriously by so- ciety, and is as important, if not more import- ant, than those who have passed beyond this stage. Besides, she is allowed to receive atten- tions such as would never have been permitted to her British sister. Dozens of young men send her flowers, boxesof " candy," and books, and everyone obligingly takes this pleasant. state of affairs for granted, not considering it a matter for gossip. One young man, however, is more attentive than any other. He calls very often in the evening, asking at the door for the Rosebud herself, not for her mother. He is good looking, well born, will inherit money, and is a " Har- vard man," but his father has insisted upon his going into business. The girl's mother is not quite sure what an American parent would do, and seeks advice of a friend with daughters. " It's all right," she is assured. " Just let things go on. Let the two dear young loeople find out for themselves whether or not they are enough in love to want to spend their lives to- gether." " But while this young man is making up his mind, my daughter will get talked about !" ex- claims the anxious mother. "Oh no, she won't," the other insists. " Don't spoil this beautiful idyll by worrying."
THE CAREER OF THE ENGAGED GIRL.

The adaptable English lady allows herself to be persuaded, and the romance goes on, at itm own sweet wilL The Rosebud " came out" in November—the commencement of the New York season—and in spring, at a country house dance, the young man proposes. The girl Las become Atheriesmized enough to be independ- ly certain that her parents will not attempt to influence her, and as she is in love, she' prompt- ly accepts. The lovers decide to keep their de- licious secret for two heavenly days, mid do so : then the young man faces the father, and is received into the bosom of the family. He gives the girl a splendid solitaire, and a little " guard " ring; she writes the news to her girl friends who are not on the spot to see for themselves , the engagement is announced ; the dazzling fun of being a debutante is over, and a new place in the Rosebud's career be- gins, that of the engaged girl. Though it is different, it is fully as delightful. If she is not in quite so much demand at balls, she knows it is only because men are afnisid they are not wanted. She can go practicallk every- where alone with her fiancé, and he can dance every dance with him if she chooses. He is al- lowed ,to take her out to dinner at a restaurant and to the theatre afterwards. Never a day passes that lie does not send her flowers, and as she was a dAbutante of 1903, when the New York fashion in these happened to be violets— always violets, great flat bunches of violets, as large or larger than a dinner plate. Roses, too, of course, with the long stems, without which roses are not roses to the American girl, and white lilacs, because she fancies they are her fel ourite flowers ; white lilacs in season and out of season, though they be two dollars spray.

div.head: LONG ENGAGEMENT.
div.p: A LONG ENGAGEMENT.

The girl's British sister was married to bet baronet after a very short engagement, because he was insistent, but the younger has learned that it avails men in America very little to be insistent, if a woman wifls differently. Most American girls like long engagements, therefore this girl decides :that she, too, will here a long engagement. She gets her way, in spite of pleadings, and plays queen to a devoted knight until autumn comes again, and a year has passed since her coining out " At Home.'' A great many of her most intimate friends have been married in the drawing-rooni of their own home under a huge marriage bell of pure white flowers. but she cannot forget English prejudiceE sufficiently to follow their example. Besides, she argues, when the idea is proposed, it church wedding is far prettier than it house wedding. At last, the day is fixed ; the invitations are sent out, and the bride-elect must not be seen gain at any public entertainment. The wed- according to the latest fashion, is to be at half past four in the afternoon, morning or evening weddings being now vierix jeu in New York society. The bride has asked six of her prettiest girl friends to be her bridesmaids, but KS her most intimate chum " has been mar- ried a few months ago, she is invited to be Matron of Honour, taking the place of Maid of Honour, an American fashion existent for some years. The bridegroom calls together X men to be his ushers, and asks his oldest friend as best man. When the girl's sister married, her baronet provided each of the bridesmaids with a brace- let ; but this being New York and not London, the bride finds that it ia her duty to buy the

div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.

If ever there was a pastime in danger of being killed by its friends, that pastime is motoring. Whilst doubt- less meaning well, there is no doubt that those respon- sible for the existence of the " Conaiderate Drivers League" have done quite as much to harm the sport as have the reckless and thoughtless chauffeurs who have brought it into aisrepute. That any motorist should have seriously supposed such a League was necessary is, to the preiudiced, strong evidence that nine-tenths of those who drive cars are hooligans or the deepest dye, whilst it is really astonishing that any but the feeble- minded should associate themselves with the scheme. To our minds, at least, it is nothing less than impertinent to urge the members to remember they are gentlemen. A gentleman is not likely to forget the fact, even if he does not belong to a League which undertakes to teach him tbe primary rules of politeness, nor, on the other hand, will the reckless chaffeur be transformed into a model of propriety by becoming a member of this gentlemanly Guild.

The Marquis of Queensberry's ill-advised application to the magistrate at the West London Police Court has already borne fruit, as indeed, was only to be expected. At Orpington, quite recently, a shot at the occupants of a passing motor car, and, only owing to the driver suddenly sprinting past when he realised the meaning of the raised gun, the occupants escaped unharmed. The assailant asserted that motorists run over children—a vague generality encouraged by a certain section of the 'daily press—and that, therefore, he should shoot them. However, the police were fetched and the subsequent appeamnne before the magistrates has resulted in him being committed for trial at the next assizes. It is a pity that bail has been allowed, for a little high-hanaed justice under the circumstances might have done much to prevent any possibility of a recurrence of carrying out the foolish suggestion made by an anti-motorist.

Every motorist will be wise if, directly he misses the invaluable driving-license and search fails to reveal its whereabouts, he makes immediate application to his County Council for a duplicate. This is sent upon receipt of one shilling, and, in the meantime, should he unluckily be stopped and asked to produce it, the fact that he had instantly acquainted the authorities with the loss, would doubtless, prevent any unpleasant • sequel. However, if this has not been done there will, in all probability, be a heavy fine to face in the subse- quent proceedings at the police court.

I An article appears in one of the weekly motoring journals dealing with the choice of a car most suitable for use at a country house, when there will be constant journeys to and from the station, and when, too, it may be called upon to tackle some stiff hills in cross-country I jaunts nhich would not be encountered upon the ordinary high roads. It is not so very long since another article appeared upon the choice of a car best I suited to the needs of a medical men, from which it is clear that people are at last beginning to realise that the type most advisable for one class of motorist would probably be utterly useless to another. The novice is far too often prone to imagine that what suits his friend must necessarily suit him, although it is obvious that, should the roads over which he will run it be ef totally different country, should he be intending to drive it himself instead of leaving it to a hired chaffenr, and so on, it is more than possible he will require something entirely different.

The twenty-four hours' trial for motor cycles took place last Saturday and proved to ho a most interesting event. Twenty entries were received and of these nineteen were actually starters. A "star " course had been selected, in order to snake the arduous work of checking, marshalling and time-keeping as easy as possible. The chosen centre was the Bull Hotel, at Watton, and each radiating arm of road measured, out and home, thirty-six miles and was to be covered in not less than one hour and fifty minutes, so that the speed limit allowed was slightly below that legally permitted.

The start was made at eight o'clock on Friday even- ing and there is no doubt some of the competitors found the night work very trying, particularly when, in addition to the unaccustomed strain of tiding throughout the hours of darkness, they had trouble with tyros or were compelled to. make some minor adjustments to their engines. Still, when twelve hours had passed there were no less than fifteen in the running. These, however, were gradually thinned out until at last only four remained for the final trip at 6 p.m. on Saturday. Of these, three survived, each having accomplished 432 miles in the twenty-four hours—the utmost limit per- mitted by the rules—bad luck befalling the fourth in the matter of a burst tyre, and, the machine being ridden in this condition, the subsequent fracture of the rim itself. The triumphant trio were Messrs. Brice on a Brown, Baddeley on a Baddeley and Woodman on a Vindec Special.

Rumours are afloat concerning a new four-cylindered car which is to sell to the public at, or near, £lB5. Undoubtedly there is going to be some very keen com- petition in the matter of small and reliable cars at a moderate price; but to our mind the wonder has been that this market was not seriously studied long before now.

div.head: Colonel Hall Walker, M.P., and the Defeat of the Government.
div.p: Colonel Hall Walker, M.P., and the Defeat of the Government.

think your readers should know that though Colonel W. Hall Walker, M.P., was absent and unpaired on that fateful Thursday, July 20th, in spite of a Government three line whip, he responds readily enough to liquor whips. He was present and voted for the liquor traffic in most of the important divisions on the liquor Traffickers' Endowment Act 1004. and on May 26th last, he was present and voted for the continuation of the drink t:affic on Sundays in England. Does Colonel Walker regard supporting the liquor traffic, its endowment, and Sabbath continuance as more important than preserving the Government ? Yours very faithfully,
CHARLES SMITH. 29, Union-street, Sheirield. Secretary British Temperance League.

div.head: Parliamentary Representation.
div.p: Parliamentary Representation.

Sir,—lt is eften boasted that the British House of Commons is a representative assembly, and that its members embody the views and the will of all classes and conditions of the nation. But a brief survey of the methods of election to that venerable Chamber, and the men elected, will suffice to demolish this pleasing fiction completely, and prove conclusively that the industrial class, which outnumbers all the others put together, has little or no representation at all. First then, as to the methods of election. It is common knowledge that even before the Writ to elect has been received, the leaders of the two great political factions take possession of the field, and dominate the whole proceedings from first to last. The people are not called together under the presidency of Mayor or Provost to quietly and seriously make choice of some worthy and respected fellow-citizen to represent them in Parliament. But with astonishing audacity the lead- ing partisans usurp this function, and select men after their own kind, not to safeguard the public well-being, but to fight the battles of the cliques. And where it happens that representatives of this type are not obtain- able locally, wandering politicians known as "Carpet- baggers " are imported from a distance to contest the seat. (There is an exemplary specimen of this kind of patriot all the way from Warrington in the Carnarvon BArghs at present.) These foreigners, of course, know nothing of the requirements and aspirations of the great body of the electors beyond the modicum that is put into their mouths by the wire-pullers. But what they lack in local knowledge is more than compensated for by torrents of eloquence which stick at nothing. Tory decries Radical, and Radical decries Tory, to such an exteut that a stranger, listening to their speeches, might be forgiven if he concluded that both parties were enemies of their common country. But there is one point, and one only, in which the wordy combatants are agreed, and that is in a studied and dignified reticence as to what the future of the legislation will be. And really they must be pardoned for this, as the fault is not theirs. Ordinary members are not expected to formulate, or even to suggest, policies. Their proper business in "The House" is as voting machines, to go after their party leaders through thick and thin,as sheep follow their shepherds. But this isnot all. So anxious to know their fate are the aspirants after Parliamentary fame that they most needs anticipate the declaration of the poll. Accordingly, bands of canvassers under the command of captains (irrrgulars I presume) are told off for the honourable duty of worming out of the sorely bewildered and indignant electors whether Nathan Smith, company promoter, or Obadiah Jones, Stickit lawyer, will be rewarded for his time and out-of-pocket money by the magic badge of M.P. and a seat at the rear of his political chief. And all this is openly and systematically done in the very teeth of the Ballot Act which was enacted to protect the electors from the prying curiosity of partisans. But,as might be expected. the ruse is not always successful. Indeed, it often happens that the figures announced by the Returning Officer and-those of the nvassers are widely divergent, to the grievous disappointment aud discomfiture of one of the candidates.

Thus much for the election process, and now for the elected. However irregular and farcical the proceedings may have been, they have resulted in a signal victory for the classes-656 stalwart defenders of monopoly to 14 humble representatives of labour. Manufacturers of all kinds, land and coal proprietors, railway and other directors, builders and owners of ships,home and foreign merchants, professional men, ,tc., Sm., have taken their seats in the Commons' House to promote and jealously guard their respective interests. But, with shame and righteous anger be it said, the millions of our brethren and sisters who are sweated from day to day in the fields, mines, factories, and on shipboard, and in other places to produce the wealth of nmney and property so largely represented in both Houses of Parliament may almost be said to have no representation at all; although in point of numbers and importance they outweigh all the other classes put together. The few labour members do raise their voices and record their votes on behalf of their oppressed and wronged fellow workers when they can, but it is impossible for them to make any headway against the solid phalanx of monopolists op- posed to them. In conclusion, workingmen may rest assured that labour leagues, and other similar inventions, under the patronage of class-aspirants to Parliament will never advance their cause ; as they are only new and thinly disguised methods for keeing them as they are at the toils of the party politicians. What they require is a broad, honest, and thoroughly independent policy of their own if they desire to make any real and lasting progress in reform. Their apathy and indifference to their own interests in the past practically delivered them hand and foot into the power of the idle and the rich who claimed to be their masters. But they were not made for such a destiny. As men and creatures of Him who is no respecter of persons they have an absolute right to their full share of the earth upon which they live, and of the kindly fruits which it produces ; while the rest due to labour should always be theirs without +curtailment. Knowing as workingmen do that the obstacles which prevent their enjoyment of all these blessings are land-grabbers, capitalists, and brewers and vendors of drink it would not be a difficult matter to bind themselves in a" solemn league and covenant "to put down these enemies at the polls, they have the power to do so if only they had the will and the wisdom to exercise it. —Yours truly, lONA.
August, 1005.

div.head: BOLD-STREET CHOIR.
div.p: BOLD-STREET CHOIR.
Presentation to Mr. Frank Hickman

At the usual weekly practice on Wednesday evening, a very interesting part of the proceedings was the pre- sentation of a large picture to the choirmaster and organist (Mr. Frank Hickman) on the occasion of his recent marriage. The picture consists of the photo of each member of the choir, arranged in a large oak frame with a photo of the organ in the centre. The SPICRETARY (Mr. C. H. Page), in a few words, said he hoped Mr. Hickman would accept the congratu- lations and good wishes of the choir, together with the present, remarking that "although not all the members were gifted with beauty, still the sentiment which prompted the gift was very beautiful." He then called on Mr. J. P. Taylor (the " father " of the choir, having been a member for 35 years) to formally present the photograph, which he did in a few well-chosen remarks.

Mr. FRANK FEICIiII-;AN in replying thanked them very much, and said he should be pleased to accept their very handsome present. He spoke of the continued harmonious feeling which existed among them, and referred to the " choir problem " which every choir- master had to deal with. This gift, he said, was only the outcome of a very sincere and loyal friendship and he congratulated the choir on their self-denial and ever-ready response to the call to duty. He was very happy to he among them and should always look with pleasure upon choir practices and presentations as., very •happy meetings. In asking the Rev. Joseph Manning to speak, he said he understood he was to have special charge of the "thumb. The Rev. G. H. Carnson (for whom the choir bad great respect) was leaving this conference and they welcomed their new minister and hoped to be able to second his eEforts in connection with the church.

The Rev. JOSEPH ATANNING Wel.9 received with applause and gave a very hurnourous account of a wedding he once officiated at and pointed the moral. He added his congratulations, and hoped the choir would try to carry their music to the highest point of perfection. He loved music and they could be sure that any effort they made would be greatly appreciated by him. He remarked upon the never-failing attendance of the choir on Sunday mornings and the splendid way they dis- charged their duties weekly, and said, however small the congregation might be, they were always sure of a good back ground which was very helpful. He wished -them all continued success.
The photos, which have been excellently taken and well-arranged, are the work of Mr. James Parkinson, of Egypt-street and will be on view in Mr. Wadsworth's shop, 59, Sankey-street, for a few days.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

West Lancashire League cricket has almost ceased to possess interest for Warringtonians. The season which opened so promisingly to the home eleven has reached a monotonous stage,for the local wielders of the willow have disappointed their supporters and successive defeats have placed them in a lowly position in the League table. On Saturday they visited Newton-le- Willows, and for the second time this season had to bow the knee to the representatives of that place. It is only fair to state that they owed their defeat in a great measure to the prowess of one player. E. M. Dowson, who has done duty for Cambridge and Surrey, and who on Saturday distinguished himself with splendid batting and bowling performances. The Warrington side, too. was weakened by the absence of the captain, E. A Connor, and it was in no very hopeful spirit that the visitors entered upon the game.

Batting first, the Warrington men put together 119. Nrason the professional, was the chief contributor, knocking up 52 in vigorous style. J. NV. Bibby (16) and W. Richardson (15)were the only other players to attain donbN figures, the majority of the batsmen having hard work in dealing with the deliveries of Dowson and Cooke. The bowling of the first named was most effec- tive, his analysis working out at 7 wickets for 45 runs.

The Newton batsmen passed the Warrington total without difficulty, their innings realizing 15S. Dowson was in grand form and compiled 75 in less than an hour His chief hits included two sixes and thirteen fours.

At present they are next to the bottom of the league table but their record is only a shade better than Prescot who have played 8 matches and have 5 points to their credit, whereas Warrington's figures are 9 matches and 6 points. Warrington second also failed to account for their Newton opponents, who triumphed iqy a 41 majority. The first part of the game was encouraging from the Warrington point of view. All the Newton men were dismissed for 1125, Wilkinson capturing seven wickets for 27 runs. The Warrington batsmen began wekl, E. Pierpoint knocking up 32 and J. T. Oliff 30 not out. The remaining players, however, did not rise to the occasion, and the inning closed for 84. -- Sankey Wire Mills are going strong this season, and still maintain their unbeaten record. On Saturday they met Winstanley Park, and ran out winners by 14. F. Taylor (20) displayed capital form with the bat, and N. Cook bowled very effectively, capturing seven wickets for 12 runs.

There was a well-contested game between Sankey Wire Mills 2nd and Wycliffe, a draw being the result. The Wire Mills were all out for 106 and Wycliffe compiled 100 for the loss of eight wickets,so that their prospects of victory, had time permitted, were very bright. For Wycliffe A. Corney batted splendidly and scored 49, while T. Whitfield (13 not out) made the best effort for the Wire Mills.

Cheshire Lines Engineers administerei a severe trouncing to Latchford Baptists. The scores— Engineers 84, Latchford o—speak for themselves. J. Duckworth was in good form with the bat snd knocked up 45, while James Monks achieved the exceptionally good bowling analysis of 7 wickets for 6 runs.
Warrington Mersey dofeated Ellesmere-street Wes- leyans by 7G, and Arpley accounted for Sankey Hall by 20.
Penketh had a ridiculously easy task in disposing of Rainhill 2nd who put together only 31 against their 175. Houghton captured four wickets for 9 runs and Shoobridge five for 13.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

The event of to-day in the world of bowling so far as Warrington is concerned is the match between Pearson and Knowles (No 1) team, and Fletchers to decide the destination of the Finlayson cup. Open to teams repre- senting Warrington works the competition has through- out been conducted in a good spirit and one which con- duced to excellent sport. The teams which are left in the final have both fought well and a close contest is promised for this (Saturday) afternoon. Both are confident of victory but the strong probability is that last years champions will claim the honours of the game and the cup will for a second year be in the possession of the Pearson and Knowles representatives, who on paper are a good 20 points better than their °pimento.

On Saturday they defeated Whitecross representa- tives by 23 points, a substantial margin on the twelve games played. The issue was never in doubt as after the first three games had been decided the victors at once obtained a lead which they gradually increased. The other match did not result in what might be termed a sporting finish the result being a foregone conclusion from the start, and a majority of 41 in favour of Fletcher's truly represented the play, Longford players winning only three out of the twelve games played.

To-day'snmatches will commence at 3 o'clock and at the conclusion, about 4.30, the Nrayor (Alderman Bolton) will hand the cup and medals to the successful team. A charge of 3d. will ba made for admission to the green.

The matches in connection with the Warrington and District League which were decided on Saturday were of unusal importance as they had considerable bearing upon the championship. Bulls Head had to visit the Penketh Park Green and it was essential, if they were to be champions, that the fixture should result in the defeat of the home team. No other result was seriously anticipated but there was the possibility that Penketh might win. It was not calculated to inspire confidence when G. Ball, an old and experiended bowler fell a victim to J. Bowyer but A. Shaw, who is probably the most expert trundler in the town,equalized matters and from that point the Church-street men never looked back and ran out winners by 33 points. Their victory places the destination of the cup beyond doubt and right well have the Bulls Head men merited the honour which is theirs.

While congratulating the winners one must sym- pathise with the losers. Poor Penketh Park! Their record is indeed a sorry one with not a single match won. Early in the season it was recognized that they were hardly class enough to compete with success with the other League teams but nevertheless they have fought gamely and shown a sportsmanlike spirit which all are bound to admire taking successive defeats in an excellent manner and smiling cheerfully in the face of adversity. The principal contestants for the second place in the League table—Fearnhead and Sankey—figured on the Fearnhead green, and the home team as was expected, succeeded in claiming the victory. They, however, had a close light and while they won, the victory was in a sense a hollow one as Sankey compiled a totat which places them in a position of greater advantage than the " farmers" by reason of their having a better scoring average.

The game was not devoid of escitingpositions. Foam- head started started by obtaining a lead of six points, but after the third game the two totals were equal. The neat game gave Sankey the lead and matters looked serious when P. Croft and J. Unsworth took the green. This borne man won handsomely and one point separated the teams the advantage being in favour of the " farmers." The home team proceeded to increase their lead and when the last two players took the green the totae stood at 132-107. Fearnhead were already congratulat- ing themselves upon a prospective victory but they were given a fright by T. Forster who, by running away from W. Weston, reduced their lead to one of eleven points. C. Roberts made a better fight with W. Ellison but was beaten and Fearnhead won by only nine points.

Altrincharn Conservative Club had their revenge on Saturday when they entertained the Sankey-street Con- servatives. When they visited Warrington they were defeated but on Saturday they turned the tables and won by 39.

A bowling main in connection with the Warrington Appollo Prize Male Choir was recently held on Mr. Nathan Cook's Green, Lovely-lane. Several very excit- ing and interesting games were played. During an interval tea was provided by Mrs. Cook, and the mem- bers thoroughly enjoyed the excellent repast. The prize winners were :-1, C. Nunnerley ; 2, Houghton ; 3, W. Critchley ; 4, A. Cook ; 5, D. Gittens ; 6, J. Wilkes ; 7, W. Woodcock ; S, H. Cook ; 9, W. Clayton ; 10, J. Green ; 11, W. Warburton ; 12, J. Davenport ; 13, J. Gibbons ; 14, G. Ratcliffe ; 15, S. Knowles ; 16, A. Greenough. One of the most enjoyable days in the choirs history was brought to a close by the singing of a number of part songs and glees.

The r4asponsible committee of the Competition is now considering the advisability of providing additional municipal bowling greens the one in Victoaia Park long fulfilled the most sanguine expectations of the supporters of the scheme. A visit to the green will show the committee the extent to which the pro- vision is appreciated and wil doubtless lead them to agree to the construction of new greens in other parts of the town.

323 306 Cycling. By the death of Mr. D. Davies, the Warrington Cycling Club has suffered a great loss, and at the funeral on Saturday the members joined in plying a last tribute of respect to one who had alwas taken an active interest in the progress of the club. The fixture of "Presidents' and Ladies' Day" was postponed, and sixty members were present at the Cemetery to witness the last rites. Mr. John Naylor (the president) intended to be present, but on Saturday had to telegraph that he as detained. Mr. Davies's cheery presence will be much missed at the club functions in which he had for years joined most heartily.
On Tuesday evening there was a fair turn out for the favourite run to Budworth via Arley and a very pleasant evening was spent.
Several tours are being organized for this week-end, and given fine weather, there will be large contingents of club members awheeel in Derbyshire and Scotland.
At the Plank-lane (Leigh) sports on Saturday J. Houghton, of Warrington, won the first prize in the half mile bicycle race and second prize in the half mile (local) race.
