div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL

The ordinary monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held in the Town Hall on Tuesday evening, when there were present :—The Mayor (Alder- man Bolton), the Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Fairclough)' Aldermen A. Bennett, John Evans, R. W. Francomb, J. Smethurst, D. Tinnion, Councillors T. H. Ashcroft, T. Barton, W. Benson, T. Burton, W. Clegg, James Evans, L. Ellison, Dr. Joseph, J. Lan, J. Maginn, P. Peacock, J. Pemberton, J. Roberts, J. Sankey, J. Skelland, J. F. Smith, F, Stott, J. Wilkinson, W. J. Wilson' T. Wright, with Messrs. J. L. Whittle (Town Clerk), A. T. Hallaway (Deputy Town Clerk), J. Fairhurst (Borough Treasurer) J. Deas (Water Engineer), J. G. Gornall (Medical , Officer), J. M. Murray (Director of Education).

div.head: PAINTING OF THE SCHOOLS:
div.p: THE PAINTING OF THE SCHOOLS:
Alderman BENNETT moved a resolution to the effect that such recommendations of the Education Committee as required the confirmation of the Council be con- ti

Councillor EurisoN seconded. Councillor WRIGHT asked jilt was ordinary asphalt- ing that was proposed to be done in the playground of one of the new schools at a cost of 3s. 5Ad. per square yard. The MAYOR said it was not ordinary asphalting, but a composition which had worked very satisfactorily at Birkenhead and was strongly recommended by the Borough Surveyor. Councillor WRIGHT said he was satisfied with the explanation. Councillor STOTT called attention to the painting of schools, Sm., during the summer holidays, and suggested that the committees concerned might consider whether some of the work in future could not be done in the Christmas holidays, as at that time many painters were out of work.
Alderman BENNETT and the IVIAYoR promised to note the suggestions and the motion was carried. snALL DWELLINGS ACQUISITION ACT.
THE LICENCE OF THE GEORGE HOTEL.

The Finance Committee reported that they considered the Borough Surveyors report upon the application of the tenant of No. 66, West-street, for an advance under the Small Dwellings Acquisition Act, 1899. It was resolved, "that the application of the tenant be not entertained." At a subsequent meeting of the com- mittee the Town Clerk submitte I a further letter from the tenant of No. 66, West-street, asking for a reduced advance under the Small Dwellings Acquisition Act, 1899. It was resolved, "that the application be not entertained."

The DEPUTY-MAYOR moved, and Councillor WiMUN- SON seconded the passing of the minutes. Councillor STOTT asked why the resolution relating to the Small Dwellings Act had been come to. The MAYOR. replied that too much was asked for the property. Councillor LORD asked what had been done with reference to the George flo+el, and if a commutdcation had been received about it.

The MAYOR said he had had no communication, and the matter was not on the minutes. It would be better to leave it alone till they had got the money. Councillor LORD : Are we likely to get the money? I understood it was refused. The MAYOR : No, no. The minutes were agreed to. THE PURCHASE OF PROPERTY IN SANKEY STREET.

div.head: RUMOURED BUILDING ON ST. ELPHI'N'S PARK.
div.p: RUMOURED BUILDING ON ST. ELPHI'N'S PARK.
"TO BUILD THERE WOULD BE A SACRILEGE." ALDERMAN'S BENNETT"S VIEWS.

The TOWN CLERK having been authorised at a meet- ing of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee to offer .C 5,000 for the purchase of the premises in Sankey-street and Legh-street from the executors of the late Rev. E. D. Garven, reported that he had agreed for the purchase of the premises at the price named. The TowN CLERK reported that he had purchased a piece of hend in Manchester-road, containing 625 square yards, from the trustees of the Clery Daughters' School for .£405,

Alderman BENNETT moved the confirmation of the minutes, and said he had pleasure in announcing that the committee had arranged with the executors of the late Rev. E. D. Garven to acquire the premises in Sankey-street and Legh-street lately occupied by Miss Garven, and with the trustees of the Clergy Institutions to buy the necessary land to widen that portion of Manchester-road which was contiguous to St. Elphin's Park to GO feet. They regarded the price asked as not unreasonable, and there would not, he thought, he two opinions as to the extreme desirability of both improve- ments. They could not afford to allow our unique municipal estate right in the middle of the borough to be spoiled by the application of any adjacent property to any unsuitable purpose; and incidentally the purchase would enable them to at once proceed with the widen- ing of Sankey-street. He only wished, as he had often said that they had fixed the width at 80 feet instead of 60 feet. With reference to the Manchester-road improve- ment it had been universally admired as far as it had gone, and the arrangements with th trustees of the Clergy Institutions would enable them to carry it a good step further. That end of the town had been too long neglected, and he was sure that when the whole of the proposed improvement was completed it would be able to offer attractions not second to any in the Borough. (Hear, hear.) A somewhat alarmist rumour had got about to the effect that the front part of St. Elphin's Park was shortly to be built upon. He could scarcely credit such a rumour. He could not bring himself to think that the sister institutions, which had lived together side by side in that locality so happily for over GO years, would fail to ultimately come to some arrangemeut, fair to each, and yet be no disadvantage to the town. To build upon that noble pleasure ground I would be a sacrilege. (Hear, hear.) St. Elphin's Park I was unquestionably one of the prettiest parts of War- rington, a veritable beauty spot, and it would be a Ithousand pities to see it turned to inappropriate uses. The committee were following the matter with close attention, and might be relied upon to use their influence in the right direction. He was sure he was expressing the opinion not only of every person in the ward but of practically everyone in the district when he said that in the interests of the Church, the College and the town alike, the park should be preserved. (Hear, hear.) Councillor EvAris seconded. Councillor STOTT said that it seemed an enormous amount to give for this land, though it might not be more than its market value. The price they had to nay for any land in Warrington was very exorbitant. The people who owned it had not made it valuable, but its value had been increased by the money which had been spent by the Corporation on public improvements. He did not know if it was the intention of the owners to sell part of it, but he hoped that if any portion of it was to be sold the Corporation would secure it for the ratepayers to be used as an open space for the locality. The MAvoit said that when a Corporation widened a road they increased the value of property for ridable purposes, and expected to get their money back. It was a matter of pounds, shillings, and pence as well as a health consideration. Alderman BENNETT agreed with Councillor Stott that it would be a pity for the land to he covered. It rested between the authorities of the two institutions, the Clergy Daughters' School and the Training College. He hoped that it would he possible for them to come to terms. If that should be so it would be preserved, for the t..wn would get the advantage of it. He thought it would be worth while to secure it at a reasonable price. There was no doubt whatever that they were the people it most fittingly devolved upon, and it was worth more to them than to anybody else. The Committee were following the progress of the matter very closely. The minutes were adopted.

div.head: ROAD FOREMANSHIP.
div.p: THE ROAD FOREMANSHIP.

The BOROUGH SURVEYOR reported at a meeting of the Paving and Sewerage Committee that Joseph Cook' road foreman' had tendered his resignation, and it was resolved, "that it be accepted, and the Borough Sur- veyor be authorized to advertise for a successor. Alderman 'DIMON, in moving the adoption of the minutes; said that the resignation of the foremarOoseph Cook, had been withdrawn, and he would remain in the service of the .Corporation. They were fully satisfied with him. Councillor ROBERTS seconded, and the minutes were adopted. THE CARNEGIE LIBRARY QUESTION.

COUNCILLOR MAGINN OBJECTS TO DELAY. The Museum Committee reported that the number of books issued from the lending library during the year ended 30th June, 1905, was 78,987, the largest previous issue having been in 1891-5. Alderman BENNETT, in moving the adoption of the minutes, commented on the record issue of books from the lending library, and said that what was alleged to be a "decaying institution "was doing a certain amount of good. Councillor ELLISON seconded. Councillor MAG INN asked if earthing had been done with regard to approaching Mr. Carnegie ? , It was time that Alderman Bennett and his commmittee were doing something, as it was now three months since the matter had been before the Council. If Mr. Carnegie were as slow over granting the money as the Museum Committee were in applying for it the library would be of no use to this generation or the next. (Laughter.) He was aware that certain gentlemen on that committee were opposed to asking 'Mr. Carnegie for anything, and others thought it infra dig for them to apply. The members of the committee had no right, however, to push their feelings on the ratepayers of the town. They did not elect themselves but were elected by and only acted on behalf of the ratepayers, and whatever their opinions might be the resolution had been passed by the Council and they had been instructed to make the application. He hoped by a month hence he would not have to make a similar charge. Alderman BENNETT said that he personally was not favourable to the application,but there were no grounds for the charges which had been made against the com- mittee. The committee were not neglecting the I matter, but giving it their serious considsration. There I

was an old proverb which said " restina lento " " hasten slowly," and the committee thought that if the committee made the application after due delibera- tion the result would be more satisfactory to all con- cerned.

Councillor MAGINN asked if Alderman Bennett would promise that something should be done this month? The MAYOR: He has promised. He will do some- thing. Councillor MAGnis : He will if he lives long enough. (Laughter.) Councillor Magian was proceeding to put a further question to Alderman Bsunett wheu the Mayor declared him out of order. The minutes were adopted.

div.head: MUNICIPAL BOWLING GREEN.
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL BOWLING GREEN.

The Borough Treasurer reported to the Town Hall. Parks and Baths Committee that the receipts from the Victoria Park Bowling Green, from the 27th June to the 19th ult, inclusive, were as follows :--1,742 tickets at 2d...414 10s. 4d. ; 791 tickets at id., 3 ss. 11d.

The MAYOR mOved the adoption Of the minutes, and said the receipts were very satisfactory. As soon as the season was over they would see what they could do in the way of extending the facilities for bowling. Alderman SMETHURST seconded. _
Councillor LORD asked if Messrs. Pickton Bros. tender for 20 park seats at 15s. 4d. each was the lowest tender? The MAYOR : Yes. The minutes were then confirmed. AUCTION SALES IN THE MARKET.
APPLICATION FOR MARKET STAND REFUSED. MINUTES SENT BACK.

The Markets Committee reported that an application from Messrs. H. Ellis Vane and Co., of Warrington, for a stand in the market on Saturdays for weekly auction sales of household furniture and effects was considered and not granted. Councillor ROBERTS proposed the adoption of the minutes, and Councillor ASHCROFT seconded.

CounCillor EVANS, speaking to the minute with regard to Messrs. H. Ellis Vane and Company's application, said he believed the IVarrington market was open to auctioneers who were not ratepayers, and he would like to know how the resolution refusing the particular application from local people was allowed to appear on the minute, and no explanation of it was forth- coming. There must be some obvious reason, unstated. for the step. He had anticipated some statement on the matter from Councillor Roberts, and he thought it was an important matter. If they were to allow auctioneers who were not ratepayers in the market, and refused a local firm, he felt compelled to ask why. He would move as an amendment that the minutes of the Committee be adopted with the exception of the one having regard to the application of Messrs. Ellis Vane and Company. Councillor WILKINSON seconded, and said he was certainly of opinion the committee had not looked upon this matter in the proper way. Men came from all parts of the globe to hold auctions and were allowed room. Yet a respectable individual living in Warring- ton was refused space. Councillor MAGINN said that the Town Clerk had informed the committee that they had no right to let that market for furniture auctions on Saturdays. It was originally meant for the sale of farm produce. The matter in its present form was soinewnat misleading, and made it appear as if permission to sell at all had been refused. That was not so. The MAYOR said that the firm had been offered Monday and had at first refused. The committee had decided that they could not grant the application for Saturday, and he understood that they had now accepted Monday. Councillor PEMBERTON supported the resolution, and was of opinion that a ratepayer of Warrington should be allowed a stand if any were allowed at all. Councillor LORD observed that he was a member of the Market Committee, but thought it was advisable to re-consider the matter.

The TOWN CLERK said it was hardly correct to say that he had informed the Committee that furniture auctions could not be allowed in the market on Saturday. He had simply mentioned that the market had been established for the sale of marketable com- modities and could not, therefore, be used for the sale of furniture.
Councillor EVANS : The point is that the market is a wholesale market.

Councillor ROBERTS said there were too many auctioneers in the market already. 'they took up so much room that the place was impassible. He did not think there were two empty stalls in the market now, and he did not know how room was to be possibly found for an auctioneer selling furniture. The MAYOR put the amendment, which was carried by 12 votes to 11. The remainder of the minutes were adopted. NEW GAS WORKS SUB-MANAGER.

The sub-committee reported on the applications re- ceived for the appointment of sub-manager and it was resolved "that Mr. W. Townsend be appointed sub- manager at a salary of £l5O per annum, the engagement to terminate by one month's notice on either side." The minutes were adopted on the motion of the DEPUTY MAYOR, seconded by Alderman EVANS.

div.head: FIRE ENGINE COMMITTEE. PROTEST AGAINST UNNECEESARY EXPENDITURE.
div.p: FIRE ENGINE COMMITTEE. PROTEST AGAINST UNNECEESARY EXPENDITURE.

The Fire Engine Committee recommended that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to advertise for a combination chemical fire extincteut, of 60 gallons capacity and also that the tender of Mr. George Venn for the supply of a set of quick hitching harness at £lB 109., be accepted. Alderman SMETHURST moved the adoption of the minutes. He was not present at the meeting of the committee and did not know that so important a matter as the purchase of the fire extincteur was coming for- ward. He thought that important matters of that des- cription should be put upon the agenda so that the members would be aware when they were to be brought forward.

Councillor BARTON seconded. 1 Councillor WRIGHT said be could not understand the chairman objecting to the resolution as the matter had been before the committee a long time. Councillor P. PEACOCK urged that it was important that the fire extinguisher should be purchased.At present they would not be able to save lives at a fire in a works on account of the length of time which it would take to get the fire escape in position. The department was about ten years behind the times and the superin- teadant admitted that everything they had got was old. Alderman Smethurst however blocked everything. Councillor EVANS objected to the purchase of the quick hixching harness. The horses came with their collars and bridles on and he therefore contended that the harness was not needed. It was one of those things they could very well do without. He did not see the use of spending £1.9 on harness which was absolutely unnecessary. He moved that the recommendations of I the committee with respect to the harness and the fire extinguisher be not approved. Councillor WILKINSON seconded. If they had horses at the fire station he would understand the need for the harness but under the prssent conditions it was not necessary. The IVIAYort : What time would he gained by the use of the harness ?
Councillor EVANS and Alderman SMETHURST : Not a second.

Councillor LORD asked if the harness would fit every horse that came. If it would not he did not see that it was any use ordering it. Alderman PrtaNcomn said they sometimes got horses 17 hands in height and others 14 hands high. The harness would not fit every horse. Councillor MAGINK supported the amendment. One of the conditions under which they hired the horses was that a pair should be kept constantly ready to be called out. They would have to take the harness off those horses and fit the other harness. Moreover horses had to be trained to go under the harness and he rather fancied that a cab horse would shie at having to do so. Until they had horses of their own he did not see that they needed the harness. Alderman SMETHURST: I think it is an entire waste of money and I withdraw both resolutions. Councillor P. PEACOCK: Don't withdraw the chemical extinguisher. Works and people are not safe with the flimsy old-fashioned implements which we have at present. Alderman SAIETIIURST : I withdraw the harness. The MAYOR suggested that the committee should he allowed to advertise for a fire extinguisher to see what it would _cost._ _
Councillor hvANs accordingly withdrew his amend- ment. s_

Councillor PEMBERTON : We want a guarantee and it will not be bought before theapproval of the Council has been obtained. Alderman SMETHURST : I will give the guarantee that it will not. The minutes were then confirmed.

"SWEET REASONABLENESS" OF THE GYMNASIUM COMMITTEE. The CHAIRMAN of the Gymnasium Committee reported that he had informed the Education Com- mittee that the members of this committee were pre- pared to meet them and consider a scheme for the gymnastic instruction of the school children. It was resolved, "That the matter be left in the hands of the following sub-committee :--The Chairman, Alderman Evans, and Mr. H. Ferguson, with full power to make all necessary arrangements." In moving the confirmation of this Alderman TINNION said he hoped the two committees would come to some agreement. Councillor CLEGG seconded.

iiii;;;;;;'dEAN''lVET-T-70S8 to speak when the Mayor asked if it was not better that he should pour oil on troubled waters. Alderman BENNETT: I desire to do something of that nature and must congratulate the Gymnasium Com- mittee upon their sweet reasonableness. Alderman TINSION said the oil usually poured out by Alderman Bennett was more offensive than ordinary oil. (Laughter.) If the Education Committee were reasonable they could come to terms. If they were not reasonable they would have to do without them. The minutes were carried. ELECTRICITY AND TRAMWAYS COMMITTEE. ALDERMAN SMETHURST AND THE STOCKTON HEATH FARE.
At a meetiug of the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee, a letter was read from Mr. Edwin Bradshaw, of

4, Egypt-street, asking if the Committee would con- sider the question of contract tickets at reduced fares on the Stockton Heath route. It was resolved that no action be taken in the matter at present. It was also resolved that return tickets be issued for use on any' esr running before 8 a.m., available for the return journey between 5 p.m. and 7 p.m. on the date of issue at the following rates :—Between Rylands-street and Stockton Heath either way, at LW. for the return journey, and between Rylands-street and Statford-road either way, at id. for the return journey. . .

Alderman SMETHURST, in proposing the adoption of the minutes, commented upon the success of the new route from Stafford-road to Victoria-square, Stock- ton Heath. He never believed that the respect- able portion of the inhabitants of Stockton Fleath would object to the payment of a 11,-d. fare to get to Victoria Square. It had turned out and the line was not the failure which some people predicted. He was doubly pleased to see that the intelligent portion of the inhabitants of Stockton Heath had decided to I pay the three-halfpenny fare. He was present at the 'meeting of the committee at which the question of cheap fares was considered and he must protest against' matters of such importance being brought forward with- out being put upon the committee's agenda. Mr. MAYOR : You were on your holidays. Alderman SMETHURST : If I had known the matter was coming forward I would have been in my place on the committee. Councillor WILKINSON seconded the minutes. Councillor EVANS referred to a minute running "That the electric cables be extended from St. Mary's-street along Knutsford-road to the Bolton Counr:il School at an estimated cost of ,C 750. He said that school would not be completed for IS months yet, and he did not think they need spend the money at present. The MAYOR said they were not making the extension particularly for the school. There had been many appli- cations for power along the way, and it was to meet that demand that they were going to put down the cables. Tne Bolton School was on)y named to fix a point. Councillor EVANS said he was satisfied, seeing that there were applications for power. The committee's recommendations were then approved.

div.head: WARRINGTON BRIDGE WIDENING.
div.p: WARRINGTON BRIDGE WIDENING.

The minutes of the General Purposes Committee con- taining the letter from Admiral Nares re the widening of the Bridge and the committee's resolution deciding to wait upon the Admiral and submit evidence in favour of the widening, were approved.

div.head: JUNIOR CONSERVATIVE GARDEN PARTY.
div.p: JUNIOR CONSERVATIVE GARDEN PARTY.
Mr. Plernoint, M.P. and the Government Defeat.

At the invitation of Mr. and Mrs. J. Charlton Parr, the members of the Warrington Junior Conservative Association held their annual garden party at Grappen- hall Heyes on Saturday afternoon. Beautiful weather favoured the event and a large number of guests assembled. Selections of music were rendered by the Pioneer Band and Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons' Male Voice Choir. Athletic sports were also held.

The prizes were distributed by Mrs. Parr, the pro- ceedings being presided over by Mr. Roger C. Parr. Mr. R. Pierpoint M.P., delivered an address. Refer- I ring to the defeat of the Government he said he need scarcely tell them that he was present in the House on that occasion duly representing them—as he hoped he always had done and would do for many years to come. (Applause.) As to the occurrence itself he did not for a moment attempt to excuse those members of the party who for their personal convenience or pleasure chose to be absent from the Division Lobby. He supposed each one of them thought that his single vote would make practically no differ- ence and expected that the other members would turn up. Unfortunately, men often thought like that in large numbers—especially in such hot weather, when it was so much nicer to be outside. Add to that circumstance the fact that the other side had carefully engineered the thing beforehand and came in in large numbers just before midnight in order to take ' them by surprise and they would see that it was not to be wondered at that sometime or other they would successfully accomplish their purpose. But was a vote of that sort to be taken as a vote of want of confidence in the Government? ("No.") There was no single member of the Government who voted on the Opposition ' side, and the small majority against them was caused 1 by the neglect—or laziness—of those members who ' ought to have been in their places. As to precedent in 1 considering whether a Government should resign on I such a vote he would remind them that Mr. Gladstone's Government was defeated over and over again and did not resign. Also, when Lord Roseberry succeeded Mr. i Gladstone as Prime Minister he was defeated, he thought, on the Address and he did not resign. Mr. Morley,in his life of Mr. Gladstone, said Mr. Gladstane could never be persuaded that Lord Rosebery's Govern- ment was anything else but pusillanimous when it resigned owing to the defeat on the Cordite Vote. Personally, he well remembered that occasion. They defeated the then Radical Government by seven, and it took him by surprise. It was perfectly certain that had Lord Rosebery'a Government chosen to retain office as they might have done they would not have been abused very much, because it was known perfectly well they would have been acting in accordance with precedent. But their position was not so weak that they were probably perfectly right in retiring. Perhaps they would also expect him to tell them something about the date of the general election. Well, if he was a prophet of great ability, he might be able to fell them, but not being that, he was afraid he could not tell them. There was plenty of work for the Government to do. To his mind, in good gobernment matters of administration were infinitely more important than matters of legisla- tion. As for example,it was swat important tint we should go on with that good understanding with Prance that we had now under the auspices o? Lord Lansdowne— (hear, hear)--and we should make firmer still our treaty with Japan, under the auspices of Lord Lansdowne and Mr. Bilfour. He hoped before long there would be a Redistribution Bill introduced. No stronger evidence could be required to show the necessity for such a measure than that furnished by the great noise of the Irish Party last week, when they elected to block private bills. That course would have stopped enor- mously the expenditure of money on work of all kinds and the Irish members very soon found out that if they carried out their threat it would make them very unpopular in the English constituencies. He hoped then, that the swollen representation of Ireland would be soon reduced to its proper level. To return again to the General Election as it affected both himself and the party, he hoped they would do all they could when the time came to return him again. (Applause.) It was not altogether for his own sake—though he had served them well.—(hear, hear)—but in the interests of the party he had the honour of representing and for the good of the country. (Applause.) On the motion of Mr. J. Fulton Smith seconded by Mr. W. L. Williams, a resolution expressing thanks to Mr. Pierpoint and confidence in the Government was adopted. Votes of thanks were accorded to Mr. and Mrs. Parr and Hr. Roger Parr.

div.head: J. GUEST GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.
div.p: J. GUEST GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

A ST. HELENS MURDER. SOLDIER'S BOGUS CONFESSION. The murder which Frederick tioardman,gunner in the Royal Garrison Artilliery, is reported to have con- fessed to was that of Sarah Flaherty, a young girl of five or six years, who was, in 1818, found dead on some waste land at the rear of Park-road, Parr. For some time after the tragic occurrence various conjectures were put forward, but no clue was obtained to the I matter. It was evidence from the state of the body that the murder had been committed several hours before the body was discovered. Boardman was questioned at Portsmouth by Detective-inspector Strong, who was sent by Chief Constable Ellerington, of St. Helens, to investigate the matter. It was found that at the date of the murder Boardman was only thirteen years of age. Since that time Boardman 11..c1 been in the hands of the S. Helens police on several occasions. About s week before the bogus confession Boardman was at St. Helens on furlough. Some time ago it was announced that Boardman's regiment had Ibeen ordered to Egypt, and it is thought that he has taken this extreme step in order to get out of the Army.

ORDER OF DRUIDS, PENKETH UNITED LODGE.---;" the monthly meeting of the above lodge, an official visit was paid by the recently appointed Grand-Master of the Order, Bro. David Houghton. A large muster of members were present in honour of the occasion, and much interest was evinced. On arrival, the Grand - Master was met at the door,according to the prescribe,d rule on these occasions, and escorted to the N.G.A.S chair. After greeting the members the lodge businesg was proceeded with, the Grand-Master presiding. members were initiated and a presentation made Bro. H. Mainley, lodge treasurer, in recognition of hig energetic services on behalf of the Order. The Grand - Master then addressed the members at some length,shd gave a resum4 of the general work of the Order, the great benefits derived, from membership of Friendly Societies, and the members will no doubt derive much benefit from his sensible, and clear advice. He wsg, loudly applauded at the conclusion of his speech. , cordial vote of thanks to the Grand-Master for visit was moved, and carried, and several member! personally congratulated Bro. Houghton en ol?r,, coming the difficulties placed in the way of his attalh ing his high odice. The lodge was thed closed.
Had the original conditions o.F automatic closure o.f Supply been in force on Wednesday night, the OPPO tion would have been in the position of being able force about 130 divisions.

"With the adoption of a system of farm colonies and similar works, there would be a reasonable Prospect of settling the unemployed problem."—Sir Albert K. Rollit. * * Mr. E. F. G. Hatch, the Conservative member of Parliament for the Gorton Parliamentary Division,has definitely announced his intention to retire at the general election "owing to the ambiguity of Mr. Balfour upon the Fiscal Question." He does not think • that Free Trade is safe in his hands and consequently ' he does not intend to stand as a Unionist candidate. How many more resignations will be sent in we 'wonder ? * * * "Take three weeks to kill them grouse and Pheasants, and then when you have got them strung up at Billingsgate Market or somewhere, come back here and do something for the poor. We will pay 70ur salaries during the three weeks—but come back!" ' Will Crooks in the House of Commons. "I sit here," said Mr. Crooks, "night after night, between , . , nine and eleven o'clock, while some Members, as they, say at cricket, are 'stonewalling,' and others are -assisting at society functions,in which I suppose there ' are fifteen courses to get through, and Members are stonewalling' till the majority arrives. It is posi- tively wicked to say there is no time."

"The Great Thel-wall "—a guess. Motor Notes. Coming Events. The annual crowning of tha Burtonwood Dahlia Queen will take place on Monday and will ha attended by the usual festivities. The ceremony is fixed for three o'clock and afterwards dances will be given by the children. The Earlestown prize band will play for dancing and in the evening a social will be held in the Board schools. The annual show in connection with the Warring- ton and District Agricultural Society will be held in Walton Park on the 17th inst. There has this year been an increase in the number of entries and the show promises to be a greater success than ever. Judging will commence at 9.30. During the day the Yorkshire Hussars' Band will play selections of music. The Football Club Sports. The great Bank Holiday attraction at Warrington will be the annual athletic sports promoted by the Warrington Football Club. An unusually interesting Tirogramme has been arranged and there should be a 'Large attendance on the Wilderspool enclosure. Prizes to the value of over R.,70 are offered and there is a splendid entry for the various events. It is ntmounced that A. Hyman,liniversity of Pennsylvania, the 220 yards amateur champion of the world, is sure to compete. The other events include a race for scholars at the local elementary schools, 150 yards handicap, one mile handicap, 880 yards handicap, one tulle and two mile bicycle handicaps, two miles walking contest &a. The Borough Brass Band will • be in attendance. A Publican's Failure. At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court on :Friday before Mr. Registrar Ridgway, John Henry Peplow,BB, Albert-road, -Blackpool, late licensed victualler, formerly residing and carrying on business at the Barn's head Hotel, Eatestown appeared for his examination in bankruptcy.—The statement of affairs alisclosed liabilities amounting to .£391 14s. 2d. and assets expected to rank at ,£.23 las. leaving a deficincy of 5.371 4s. 2d —The bankrupt attributed his failure to want of capital, bad trade, and heavy business expenses in proportion to turnover. In answer to Mr. Johnson, deputy official receiver, the bankrupt stated that the chic f reason why he received notice from the brewery company was because Lord Newton's agent had complained that he had not , 'cooked a leg of mutton properly.—During twelve I months he lost £5O in betting. He lost :£3O on the Derby.—Debtor was also questioned by Mr. H. J. Langton, on behalf of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., and Mr. F. G. Taylor, for Messrs. Gilbert and John Greenall, Limited.
